subsubtopic: TABLING OF CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION 1970 CAPITAL BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement on the capital budget of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the calendar year 1970 which for the first time is being tabled this early in the year. The approved capital budget authorizes CMHC to make loans under the various sections of the National Housing Act in a total amount of $854 million. This represents an increase of $174 million over the 1969 commitment level of $680 million. As in 1969, and in accordance with the undertaking given in the Speech from the Throne at the opening of this session, the largest part of the corporation's budget will be devoted to the provision of housing for low-income families and persons. A total of $570 million has been reserved for this purpose.
An amount of $265 million has been allocated to the provincial housing authorities for the public housing program under section 35 of the National Housing Act. They were so informed last week. In almost all cases, this matches provincial requests. An amount of $105 million will be directed immediately to section 16 loans to sponsoring groups who will supply low-rental housing in limited-return, non-profit and co-operative projects. The sum of $200 million is being reserved temporarily for new innovations and a balancing of distribution based on need. It is my hope that a substantial portion of this $200 million can be used to bolster efforts in those areas where poverty is most acute and to employ new or revised techniques for reaching low-income families where the present arrangements under the National Housing Act may not be fully effective. In any event, these funds will permit the corporation
to arrange in 1970 for the construction of
35.000	housing units specifically for low-income families.
So that hon. members will have some idea of the magnitude of this allocation it should be noted that during the 20 years prior to 1969, 82,000 homes for low-income families were built in Canada through the CMHC loan budget. In 1969, in line with government policy, provision was made for 27,000 units of low-rental, low-income housing in that year, a number that will be increased to not less than
35.000	units in 1970.

The total allocation of capital funds for low-income housing in 1969 and 1970 at 62,000 units therefore represents 75 per cent of the previous 20 years' performance. In addition to the specific low-income housing sections, $110 million will be for direct loans under section 40 to home owners for new and existing housing in small towns, rural areas and the remote parts of Canada where new communities are emerging as a result of the development of resource industries. It is my intention, Mr. Speaker, that the direct lending activities of CMHC under section 40 shall also be devoted to the needs of families in the lower income brackets.
An allocation of $45 million has been made for student housing, which will provide 6,500 dormitory beds on university campuses. Unfortunately, this allocation will not meet all of the demand for student housing in 1970. But in view of the pressing and greater need for housing for low-income families and because of the large amount of capital funds directed to student housing in recent years, it is my opinion that a modest decline from $55 million to $45 million this year is appropriate. In this regard hon. members will recall that $340 million has been devoted to student housing in the last nine years, an amount that has produced more than 56,000 hostel beds and nearly 5,000 units of fully served accommodation on university campuses.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION 1970 CAPITAL BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the statement by the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing. It certainly shows some awareness of housing problems as they affect the poor. But I must state at the outset that we on this side of the House are extremely disturbed and gravely disappointed that the minister has made no mention of guidelines for public housing, which are extremely important to all. Therefore it appears that uncertainty still remains regarding size and design. I hope that the minister, in his wisdom, will look into this matter inasmuch as several questions have been directed to him over the past months as to when these guidelines would be available.
One very important point regarding the minister's statement which gives those on this side of the House some concern is the fact that, as has been said on many occasions, tenants in public housing are trapped by high rents. We must remember that public housing was never intended to be permanent but rather only a temporary means of providing housing for those at the bottom of the economic ladder until such time as they are able to move into more substantial housing on a permanent basis.

I should like to point out at this time that those living in public housing who earn approximately $560 a month pay rent of approximately $160 a month. As their income increases we find that those making approximately $600 a month pay $180 a month for rent. Yet studies have shown that people living in our larger metropolitan areas where the same circumstances exist who earn $14,000 a year pay approximately $176 per month for rent. Therefore I point out to the minister that the public housing rental scale is far too high. Changes must be made to take account of differences in projects, in construction costs and in the quality of services. In this regard we have to pay specific attention to the tenant associations which are deeply involved in this matter.
I notice the Minister mentioned that some emphasis is to be placed on limited dividend housing. I point out that with $105 million to be devoted to this field we must have some regard for priority. In effect I do not think this type of home is geared to meet the needs of those in the lower income bracket but rather the needs of those in the $6,000 to $8,000 bracket. Therefore I say we should be concerned to see that at the expiration of 15 years these limited dividend housing projects will have no further governmental supervision. Charges of $100 a month for a one-bedroom apartment could conceivably increase to $200 a month.
With regard to limited dividend housing we must also be concerned about the high cost of land. In order for this type of project to be successful it is important that the government realize that we must be concerned about acquiring serviced land upon which this type of housing can be erected. We have to realize that public housing is designed to meet the needs of the poor. Therefore our policies with respect to public housing should be directed to assisting those people whom I have described as being locked in.
The amount of money now going into direct loans is of some significance in terms of the interest shown, but I would like to remind the minister that in the past-and here the only figures we have are for 1968-apparently 75 per cent of this money was directed to people who on average were making between $8,000 and $10,000 per year.
There were certain unwarranted inconsistencies in the minister's speech which I would like to bring to his attention. One concerns the fact that the government does not have an acceptable urban renewal policy. The vast
February 2, 1970

majority of poor people in this land live within areas now designated for urban renewal projects. The minister's statement on this aspect is unacceptable to many people, particularly to those on this side of the House who are concerned about helping the poor. I say with all respect to the minister that he should try to issue a policy statement at least once a year.
I believe that the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) should get together with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). It appears to me there is not too much rapport between them, if that is now the acceptable word rather than dialogue, because the Minister of Finance wants to bring homes under a new capital gains tax structure, while at the same time he is talking about taxing the small businessman at the rate of 50 per cent on his profits, a step which will certainly discourage home ownership.
I must also point out that student housing is a unique problem calling for special consideration. It has been reported that there will be some 500,000 students needing accommodation by 1975. If this be true, then we must be very concerned because student housing affects the intellectual and emotional development of students. A sum of $45 million is neither practical nor adequate.

I welcome the statement of the minister. I point out, however, that successful public housing is not only dependent on the number of projects but also on the inter-related effect of general housing policy. subsubtopic: TABLING OF CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION 1970 CAPITAL BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amiable and courteous minister read his statement with a great deal of pride, I
CMHC 1970 Budget
thought. I suppose he ought to be congratulated that he did make the statement today. I remind him, however, that this is the beginning of February and that the Ontario government found it necessary to freeze its public housing program until he had tabled the CMHC budget. I see no reason in the world why he could not have done so before the end of last year instead of in the second month of the year to which the budget is intended to apply.
Everyone in this House and in the country must be glad that the minister has increased the money available for public housing in view of the fact that this is the major concern in the generally difficult field of housing. But I cannot help but be distressed and saddened by the fact that after some years of study of the problem of housing, after task forces, reports and housing conferences across the country, all we have today is the provision of a little more money in the realm of housing. Have any guidelines for public housing, any of those programs necessary to make it effective, any of the details, been made known to this Parliament, the provincial governments or the municipal authorities? What in heaven's name are we going to do for the poor people who have no housing? That is where the problem lies.
I happened to be present last Saturday, as was my leader, the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands, at a meeting at Trefann Court in Toronto where people concerned with urban renewal and threatened with the demolition of their houses, and people from existing public housing projects such as Regent Park, met with us and spoke of their worries. It was an experience to sit and listen to these Canadians speak of the kind of life they sire forced to live in these public housing projects. Apparently the attention paid to garbage collection in these large apartments is inadequate and in some cases garbage is piled up at elevators to within two feet of the ceiling. Apparently, too, the people cannot always get adequate maintenance service and have to chase around for days to get plumbing or electrical repairs made. They complain too that the rents are much too high for people with families to support.
One cannot feel satisfied that the public housing program up to this time has accomplished anything except to provide a roof over heads that might otherwise not have had one. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is not what we are after. Surely what we are after is to build communities into which Canadians who

February 2, 1970
CMHC 1970 Budget
cannot afford high-price homes can move and live in decency and with some sort of personal fulfilment rather than having to live in a new form of degradation, a new form of inferiority such as accompanies these public housing projects.
These people told us that they have no recreation facilities, no chance of participating in what takes place in the projects and that there is bad management. I am just reporting what they told us. I appreciate that the federal minister does not do the managing. That is done through the Ontario Housing Corporation or similar bodies in the other provinces. I am not saying it is directly his fault but I am saying that it is his fault to some extent because the government has failed to bring down guidelines for public housing demanding that there be recreational facilities and good management and laying down as a condition governing the advancing of any money the requirement that the environment be such that Canadian children can be brought up in decency. That is the main point I wished to make.
I do not wish to speak at such length that Your Honour will have to remind me to be brief. I say to the minister that what he has presented today is really no solution to those concerned about the problem of public housing. The problem is a social one. It is of concern to those living in our present public housing projects who cannot live in decency and have to pay too high a rent. Many of these people are not given any chance to make decisions which will affect their lives in these apartments.
I submit that the minister is doing only one-tenth of his job when he brings to our attention the slight and inadequate increase in the allocation of funds for public housing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be quite brief. I merely wish to point out some gaps in the government proposal on housing. Each time that the government announces that it is granting some kind of assistance, I wonder what it really means for Quebec. We already know that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation provides very few loans to Quebec compared to Ontario. This depends on the fact that standards in a country as vast as Canada cannot be the same for all provinces. In the housing field, some provisions are closely related to the individual himself.
Due to the presence of various ethnic groups in Quebec, in comparison with other

Canadian provinces, the government should have realized that there was already a housing corporation in that province which cannot have the necessary scope to serve the people, on account of its lack of funds. In order to solve the problem, should the government not have provided more money to the Quebec housing corporation, and thus by decentralizing the problem, it could more easily have met the needs of the population of Canada in general and that of Quebec in particular.

I appreciate your assistance, Mr. Speaker. One factor that has not been covered in the 29 points concerning safety factors in the United States, and which is unique to Canada, concerns our weather conditions. All the cars that one sees stalled on the Queensway, and on all the other highways and byways because of weather conditions, are an added hazard to traffic in wintertime, a hazard that does not exist in most of the United States. These stalled cars cause many serious accidents in Canada.
When a slight drizzle and foggy conditions are forecast, one can expect an increase in the number of road accidents. On cold mornings there will probably be as many rear-end collisions on the Queensway, even on dry pavement, as there are when conditions are slippery, so slippery as to make stopping impossible. The fact that some cars will not
Motor Vehicle Safety
run in this type of weather adds to the seriousness of the problem.
In the United States, it is reported that the cost of installing mandatory safety devices on cars came to $46, but a sum of $107 was charged to automobile purchasers. It is interesting to note that a survey of motorists disclosed that 54 per cent of those 20 to 49 years of age indicated a willingness to pay a higher price for safety devices, but only 50 per cent of those over age 50 indicated a similar willingness. I believe if drivers aged 60, 65 and 70 had been surveyed, a majority would have indicated a marked degree of reluctance to pay for additional safety features.
No doubt this bill will be examined thoroughly in committee. Members may draw attention to studies done in the United States which indicate that 10 per cent of safety devices produced by United States factories are rejected as unsafe following inspec.ion. Members will certainly hope this will not be the case in Canada.
No doubt members will also raise the question of car bumpers. I am sure that even if a motorist in Toronto had a piece of steel railway track welded all around his car he would still not find it safe to drive on some of the freeways there. It appears most car bumpers are installed just for wives to polish. They certainly are not installed for protection.
When I looked at the bumper on a car I previously owned I was amazed to see a big dent in it. I was sure I had not hit anything, and that nothing had hit me. When I looked at a number of similar type cars, I found they all had a dent in the same place. Another example of this was the little Karmann Ghia Volkswagen. It always had a dent in the hood. This was not because I drove it under a truck, but simply because the bumpers did not coincide.
I like the advertisement, although I do not believe it, which shows a guy with a sledge hammer banging upon a car bumper, and nothing happens to it. Such a bumper might withstand a five or ten miles per hour impact, without everything being scattered all over the pavement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
If a little more cobalt were put in the bumper, it might produce a stronger alloy and make it last longer. That would help some of the mines in my area.
Another reason I have for speaking on the bill today is that it makes no provision with

February 2. 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
respect to snowmobiles and snowmobile safety. The snowmobile is one of the greatest inventions the Canadian people have seen in many years, and many people are riding them for sport. I noticed the other day that two old ladies, one over 70 and the other over 60, were out on their snowmobile and ran into a car. Clearly, people of mature years as well as those not so mature are using snowmobiles which are growing in popularity. For that reason, I think it will be necessary for us to introduce legislation governing the safety of snowmobile operation. This matter comes under federal jurisdiction. I am also pleased to note that, since snowmobiles in large part are manufactured in Canada, the regulations governing their safety can be brought under federal jurisdiction. I have a number of suggestions to make with respect to the safety of snowmobiles.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
You know, Mr. Speaker, one cannot believe everything one hears about horsepower. It seems to me that some manufacturers lie like the dickens when they speak about the horsepower of their cars. You see tractors rated at 15, 20 or 25 horsepower, and yet you will see a Buick rated at 450 horsepower. The Cadillac people now have on the market a car with a motor said to develop 500 horsepower. A few years ago, an engine of that size would power an aeroplane of some size; it was enough to run a diesel plant which would supply electric power for a town of some 10,000 inhabitants. Clearly, when manufacturers talk of horsepower they are not talking about the power you can use to pull your neighbour out of the ditch; they are talking about concepts of speed and weight.
Advertising of a similar sort is applied to snowmobiles. These little vehicles are about 6 or 7 feet long, probably 2 or 3 feet wide, and weight anywhere between 250 and 1,000 pounds. They are now powerful enough to reach speeds of between 105 and 115 miles per hour. Of course, these fast snowmobiles are basically ordinary machines which have been souped-up, to use the vernacular. I think the minister ought to interest himself in this area and try to inform the public of the dangers through a program of advertising. As I say, horsepower really has little to do with how much power you have to pull your neighbour out of the ditch or pass the car ahead of you. It is based on engine capacity and the type of gasoline you use. I think our advertisers have been emphasizing the wrong

things when advertising snowmobiles. The size of snowmobile power plants ought to be limited by law, and there ought to be some distinction between snowmobiles used on the race track and those used for every day purposes.
Another problem is the noise of snowmobiles. Although some municipalities have bylaws governing noise, those bylaws are difficult to enforce insofar as snowmobiles are concerned. I know that some municipalities say snowmobiles may not be used in city streets, yet these snowmobiles which are kept at home must pass through city streets on their way to the country or to open spaces. One of my constituents complained about noisy snowmobiles going past his window on Sunday mornings. On the morning in question he tried to watch television but, because of the noise from snowmobiles outside, he could not do so. He went to the window and within one hour had counted 82 snowmobiles going past his house. In a subsequent letter he told me that he became more disturbed on learning that wheels could be fitted to snowmobiles, enabling them to be used in the summer as well as in winter. Clearly, some kind of engine muffler must be fitted to snowmobiles. You are not allowed to drive a car in any town without an engine muffler; neither are you allowed to operate a power lawnmower without some kind of muffling device. The same sort of regulation ought to apply to snowmobiles.
The question of headlights is also important. People approaching a snowmobile on the highway at night very often cannot tell if the vehicle approaching is a motorcar with only one headlight, a motorcycle or a snowmobile. Just as we would not appreciate hearing, say, 200 Model T Fords going by without engine mufflers, so I submit our motorists do not appreciate meeting vehicles in the dark with only one headlight. It is often impossible to tell, as I say, whether the vehicle you are meeting is a car with only one headlight. Sometimes a motorist may think he is meeting a car which has only its left headlight working. Clearly, if he pulls to the side of the road in order to take evasive action he may be doing the wrong thing if the approaching vehicle turns out to be a snowmobile. I, therefore, advocate that for snowmobiles as well as for motorcycles, two headlights set fairly close together ought to be mandatory.
My next point has to do with the survival of those who may be stranded in the bush. This ought to be of particular interest to the
February 2, 1970

Department of Transport. Very often these days, snowmobiles travelling in the bush break down. In temperatures of between 30 below and 40 below zero, it is often impossible for a man to survive in the bush unless he is equipped with snowshoes, knowledge of the environment and survival equipment. This equipment ought to include an axe and, I submit, some sort of radio oscillating device costing about $20 which could be switched on and guide rescue forces to him. Snow conditions in the bush often make it impossible for a man to walk far. If he could switch on some kind of oscillating device, which could work on the citizens radio band or a police band, his rescue would be more easily directed. These bands, for instance, could be monitored on a continuing basis, so that in an emergency we would not have to wait until a person was known to be lost before setting rescue operations in motion. We could provide adequate penalities in case children played around with such devices.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Of course, repairing one of these devices would probably cost as much as the original purchase price, but nevertheless it should be on the machine. It should be sealed so that once it is turned on it cannot be turned off until the rescue is effected. If this simple device were installed in an aeroplane, one could locate the aircraft very quickly. It has a range of 20 miles and is operated by a flashlight battery on one particular band. I understood they were to be installed on aircraft so that if a crash occurred, causing an impact of a certain magnitude, this device would automatically start operating.
There are several other considerations, Mr. Speaker. I am sure the municipalities will have to give consideration to installing guy wires parallel to the roads. I heard of a girl who was riding behind her boyfriend on a skidoo who ended up with his head in her lap after hitting a guy wire. A friend of mine, skidooing on his own farm, hit a barbed wire fence and had to have 40 stitches put in his face. He nearly lost an eye. Imagine what could happen when one is not familiar with the terrain! This bill may be concerned with safety devices such as roll bars or reinforced windshields. In the case of skidoos, we have an opportunity right now to make safety devices of this type available to the public before any more damage is done. It is no use waiting until a dozen people have their heads tucked under somebody else's arm.
Motor Vehicle Safety
We have this opportunity, and I think the minister is well advised to follow the American safety program in the initial stages. In Canada, perhaps we are more interested in a car that will operate safely and satisfactorily in northern climates. Features such as rear window defrosters, battery chargers and block heaters are much more important to us than some of the smog devices installed in California. Perhaps, we should consider these as well, but there are some purely Canadian problems on which we will have to act independently of the United States.
I am not sure what we should do about studded tires. In the United States, 10 per cent of the tires tested failed in one out of six tests but I am not clear how many of these failures were related to heat or cold. You will remember that after the war everybody was begging, borrowing or stealing tires because they were in short supply. On a cold morning it was not unusual to find all four tires flat. They were just not made for cold conditions. Perhaps studded tires are a northern problem, but they are costing provincial taxpayers large amounts of money if the report on highway damage is correct. The tungsten studs appear to be fine for the first snowfall, but I am not sure of their effectiveness in deep snow or ice. The safety requirements for tires in Canada would be totally different from those of the United States. Tires should be tested under Canadian winter conditions and the results would probably differ greatly from tests conducted in the United States.
The minister has shown some initiative in presenting this bill, as have some members in drafting private members' bills. One is my colleague from Surrey (Mr. Mather) who has had experience with the National Automobile Associations and has been interested in promoting highway safety for quite some time. The fact that the minister has taken some of the better points from a number of bills, and that there has been some Canadian consideration of this problem, leads me to believe that the minister will give consideration in committee to the extension of this investigation into some other fields, particularly snowmobiles and water safety. I am very surprised how many people wearing life-preserving equipment bearing the stamp of approval of the Department of Transport lose their lives. Some improvement could be brought about in this bill.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL MARKS AND STANDARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-137 introduced a day or two ago by the Minister of Transport is a very important bill.

February 2, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
I should like to make a few suggestions which I trust will be accepted by the House, particularly in view of the fact that I spent some 23 years in law enforcement and came in contact with some of these problems under the most distressing circumstances. It is a disgrace that in North America we kill upwards of 60,000 people every year on our highways, not to mention innumerable cases of impairment, maiming and property damage running into millions of dollars. No law can stop this, but it certainly is a step in the right direction.
As we all know, it is very difficult to enforce law because once the manufacturer has sold the automobile to the public, often he feels that is where his responsibility ends. This bill, Mr. Speaker, purports to plug one or two of those gaps.
It may be dangerous to have safety stickers or safety marks put on automobiles by the manufacturer because sometimes these automobiles are defective when they leave the factory. The previous speaker mentioned bumpers, and everyone who drives an automobile knows that the present bumpers are entirely inadequate. A bumper should be able to absorb the shock of an automobile running into a solid object at 30 miles an hour without danger to the automobile. We cannot be sure that there will not be danger to the occupants, but shock absorbers or a properly built bumper would reduce damage both to the automobile and the occupants.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I see no reason why a safety sticker should be put on an automobile when the bumper, one of the most important parts of the automobile when it is in motion, is nothing more than a piece of tinsel. Although it is extremely high priced, it is absolutely useless for the job for which it is intended. The amount that we pay for these chrome beauties could very well be used for devices made from reinforced rubber and steel. There could be some form of shock absorber or oil recuperating system similar to the one on large guns which we had in the army. The modern automobile is as lethal a weapon as a piece of artillery. The committee should give priority to bumpers when considering safety factors.
Some attention should be given to the danger caused by frost. I do not see any reason why windshields could not be lined with an arrangement of very fine heating wires to keep them free of frost. In cold climates such as we have in Canada, I suggest this should be mandatory for all windows.

It has always seemed strange that trucks are obliged to have all sorts of safety devices, but these are not mandatory on automobiles. One such item that comes to mind is a proper flasher. Most automobiles today have a flasher system, but this becomes inoperative when the battery goes dead. I think a mandatory provision should be incorporated in this bill that every automobile should have a double safety feature. If the electrical flashers are inoperative, there should be manual devices such as fire flares or the ordinary battery operated flashers. These flares could be put out for protection when changing a flat tire or if the vehicle is abandoned in a snowdrift with part of the car protruding. These flares could be used any time the automobile is a menace to traffic.
It should be mandatory that all automobiles have a proper towing hitch on both the front and rear of the car. When a vehicle becomes stalled in traffic which is proceeding at 60 miles an hour, it immediately becomes a menace. There should be a steel hook for towing purposes located in an accessible location so that it is not necessary to crawl underneath the car. The vehicle could then be towed by another vehicle with a strong nylon cord or chain.
I am sure law enforcement officers would support me when I say that many serious accidents occur after some minor breakdown, such as a flat tire, running out of gas, becoming stuck in a snowdrift or on the icy slope of a hill. The danger arises when people are on the highway trying to get the vehicle clear. Often, another vehicle comes over a hill or cuts out from other traffic and collides with the stalled vehicle.
Perhaps all these safety features cannot be incorporated at one time, but I feel they are long overdue. I feel they are necessary if the vehicle is to receive a government approved safety sticker. The only argument against these features at the moment is their cost. I feel there should be a little less soap opera advertising, and more value and safety for the purchasers of these vehicles.
I am glad the minister contemplates spending some government money on research. If we are to have safety devices, then by all means we should have our more intelligent people working on the cheapest and most effective devices so that the cost can be kept to a minimum. This would give some of our bright young people an opportunity to pursue this matter in the Canadian research councils, universities and in the automobile factories.
February 2, 1970

I am delighted to see that a step forward is being taken on the question of pollution. A day or two ago I made a gloomy speech on this subject. I pointed out that our atmosphere is being endangered by the emission of an enormous quantity of exhaust fumes, and that perhaps we are destroying forever our very limited oxygen supply. I think there should also be research on this subject. A great deal could be done to ensure that the most efficient fuels are used in our automobiles, such as those hydrocarbon fuels which create the least carbon dioxide and use the least amount of oxygen to propel the vehicle.
There has been a great improvement in storage batteries. Such batteries might well be incorporated into a vehicle as a subsidiary electrical driving device. This would be valuable on long trips. When driving from here to Toronto, upon reaching the outskirts of Toronto this electrical device could be switched on and used to drive through the city where the problem of pollution is the greatest. This system would not be necessary when driving in the country where the vehicle would be using up oxygen, but not endangering the health of the people.
This whole matter of safety on the highways is not confined to Bill C-137. There should be a continuing, concentrated educational program which could also be used to teach our children safety values. Safety programs can be effective. I hope hon. members will forgive an old man for reminding them of a situation which occurred in 1938 and 1939 in greater Winnipeg. Even in those days, the population of that city was 350,000. By co-operaiion of the public and the police, a safety record was established, which I think is an all time world safety record, of 228 days without a fatal accident-two-thirds of a year without anyone being killed. I have no hesitation in saying that if one picks up the newspaper today or tomorrow, there will be a report of a fatal accident in the greater Winnipeg area. I believe this to be true of any major city. In this instance, there was a period of eight months without a fatality. The automobiles of that day were very much the same shape and size as those of today. I do not think the driving public were greatly different. They were hurrying home for their dinner, and many of them used alcohol. However, with a concentrated effort, co-operation between the police, the local authority and those responsible for the administration of the law, a magnificent safety record was set up and there is no reason why any other city cannot equal it or do better.
Motor Vehicle Safety
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
We have better machinery today, better safety facilities. It is true that automobiles are more powerful but they are equipped with better safety devices-better brakes, power steering. Often there is two or three times as much contact between the automobile and the highway, resulting from the use of much wider tires.
Then, there is the question of what can be done by concentrating on safety. Speaking as a former police officer, I believe the first responsibility rests on the law enforcement officers. I know there are certain roads in Canada today which are considered to be revenue lanes the public is reluctant to drive down them for fear of being picked up for some picayune traffic offence. Motorists figure they are paying the cost, to the municipality, of running the police force. This results in bad liaison between the police and the public. If the minister, and all hon. members present will take cognizance of what I am saying and use their influence in the right way to make sure this sort of attitude is discouraged, I think the result would be beneficial. There is nothing in my opinion, next to the courtesy of one man toward another, which prevents accidents on the highway so much as a proper respect for the law. I admire a police force which enforces the law, but it should not engage in a game of hare and hounds in which it is continually hounding the public. The force is there to serve the public, to make sure that traffic flows properly back and forth. It is a sad thing when motorists get the idea that they are being forced, by a police force which is not doing its proper job, to pay municipal taxes that is, by a force which is raising revenue instead of making the highway safer.
I want to say something about the breathalyzer test. I have always been a strong supporter of civil rights and liberties, but when we are killing up to 60,000 people a year on the highways I say it is time we all put false pride in our pockets and said: If I have been drinking so much that the policeman thinks I am drunk, I owe it to the public to blow into the little balloon. It is a question of co-operating in the effort to reduce this terrible toll of our highways. Let us hear no more about motorists being assaulted when asked by the police to take this test. Instead, let each motorist resolve not to be one of those who carelessly risk other people's lives because

February 2, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
they insist on mixing gasoline and alcohol. I believe the breathalyzer test is a very fair experiment.
People have told me that with .08 per cent of alcohol in their bloodstreams they are just as capable of driving as if they had not taken any alcohol, or just as capable of driving as anyone else. I challenge this assertion. If they could see the films made of drivers who thought they could drink and still drive well, or the safety films put out by the research institutes, I am sure they would be convinced no one is safe behind the wheel of a car travelling at 60 miles per hour when he has .08 per cent of alcohol in his system.
It is not alcohol alone which is entirely responsible for the high death toll. I bring the word down: the word I should like hon. members to take home with them is "courtesy". It is when alcohol is mixed with bad manners that it is most explosive. When alcohol is added to bad manners, and the motorist gets out on the highway with a tired, jaded feeling, determined to hog the road and race the other fellow home, the combination is often fatal. In all the years I was a policeman I cannot remember a fatal accident involving two cars when alcohol was not involved in the case of either one or both drivers. I did not always find physical evidence in the form of bottles, or alcohol in the cars, but I cannot recall any fatal accident-and I was present at far too many-when there was not at least a strong suspicion of impaired driving on the part of one or both drivers involved. This, in itself, should be sufficient justification for accepting the breathalyzer test. Surely, we owe it to others to drop the keys into the mailbox after we have been drinking, or to give them to the wife and let her drive home.

speechtext: She may be drunker than you.

Money might well be spent on public education, or on the provision of safety awards. I like that idea. When I read that a bus or truck driver has won a 20-year safety award I am ready to take my hat off to him. Anyone who can drive through our cities and on our highways for 20 years, or cover a million miles without an accident, has got to be a superman. When these drivers have travelled a certain number of miles I suggest they might even be considered for one of the Canadian awards. To me, a bus driver who has driven two million miles without an accident is a public hero who deserves not only to be honoured but given a salary increase of 20 per cent. Some wonderful films are available.

Our national research people, the Mounted Police and the municipal police all have films on road safety which deserve the widest publicity. Everyone in a position to make use of them should draw out these films and show them at service clubs or at scout meetings.
I should like to see a reinstatement of the old youth and police programs begun by the Mounted Police some 25 years ago. Members of the force who were then, and still are, very highly respected, especially among young people, spent a great deal of their own time, with a minimum of assistance from the government as to time, vehicles at their disposal and the use of films, talking to young people and showing them films-how the force trained their dogs; how they made policemen; the kind of policemen who were true servants of the public, out to maintain the safety and happiness of the public. And they very much resented this modern trend of using the policeman as a revenue officer. It should never be done, and whenever it is done it should be discouraged.
This bill will go to the committee. I, for one, think the committee system has some very valuable uses, though it is still in the experimental stage. Let us get hold of this bill, take the 29 main points which the minister has outlined, examine them carefully and enlarge upon them. It might be well to spend a little money on research and upon the education of the public, because the prevention of automobile accidents is far more important than anything we can do after they have occurred.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I close by reminding you once more that in 1938 Winnipeg managed to get through two thirds of the year without one fatal accident among 350,000 people. If that could be done then, it can be done again now. The money that was spent in those days represents only a very small proportion of the amount of money we are spending every day to clean up this mess after it has occurred.

While this bill is a very timely and important piece of legislation, as many hon. members have pointed out it lacks teeth and effec-

tive administrative measures to cope with the serious problems it was designed to alleviate. This bill merely seems to be a copy of United States safety standards, and a governmental compliance with standards already effected by most major car companies. There is no real, clear evidence of a truly Canadian safety standards code, in spite of the fact the department has allegedly been deeply involved in a comprehensive research program to determine and prescribed various minimum safety regulations and standards for vehicles operating in Canada.
Some of the safety devices we now have on our automobiles as standard equipment may be effective. Some, on the other hand, raise some degree of doubt, perhaps not totally in principle, but in design. For example, it was just last week that the Winnipeg police department removed the headrests from their patrol cars as a safety and convenience measure. This was done for safety because the officials of the department found the design of the headrests to be a hindrance to vision which more than offset the appreciable protection factor for which the headrest was intended.
I could also refer to the use of seatbelts. In a recently conducted survey in the province of Alberta it was found that only 18 per cent of the motorists interviewed actually used their seatbelts, in spite of the fact they knew of their existence and were aware of their function. If a motorist is grossly endangering his life or health by not using seatbelts, then' perhaps we should consider legislation forcing the use of this device. The use of any safety innovation such as this should be enforced if it is to be effective. If, on the other hand, only 18 per cent of the motoring public choose to use this device, with no indication of a possible increase in usage, it then would appear to be merely another factor contributing to the cost of manufacturing a car. This being the case, then the customer should be given the choice of purchasing a car with or without seatbelts. Seatbelts could be considered an option rather than mandatory item to be included in the price of the automobile.
Having regard to the stepped-up research program to which the minister referred, I must say Canada could certainly stand some improvement in this area. In substantiating this fact, I should like to point out that not so long ago the two-ply tire was introduced as standard equipment on all passenger cars and light trucks. This tire was to be safer because it supposedly had all the qualities of a four-ply tire plus many other side benefits. It was
Motor Vehicle Safety
to have been safer because it ran cooler; it was to have been shock-resistant and impact resistant because it was more flexible and had a tougher core, and it was supposed to give longer wear. In short, it was totally engineered to meet existing highway travel demands, freeway operation, gravel and dirt roads. The simple fact is that this tire was not only unsatisfactory in a performance or economy sense, it was totally unsafe. It was not long before blowouts, ruptures and separations became a rather common occurrence.
The interesting point I should like to bring to the attention of the House relates to the great selling job that automakers and tire manufacturers did in the United States and in Canada, particularly with the governments. They fell for this so-called revolutionary breakthrough, hook, line and sinker, and without hesitation placed their designated mark of approval on these tires to indicate that they met government safety standards.
After these so-called "rags" appeared, as they were commonly referred to in automotive circles, it was not long before the consumer found that these tires were totally unsatisfactory, unsafe and uneconomical, not only to the consumer but likewise to those involved in merchandising the product. The automotive makers found themselves in the embarrassing position of having to make a complete circle in their recommendations by recommending four-ply tires to correct a steering condition which developed from the use of this ardently supported two-ply tire.
The concern and lack of acceptance by customers resulted in a situation wherein new vehicle customers refused to accept a new car with a two-ply tire of any brand name and simply demanded a safe four-ply tire. These were furnished at an additional cost of from $50 to $75. The result was an insurmountable buildup of two-ply tire stocks within many wholesale and retail tire outlets. Eventually, tire companies refused to take their own tires back in exchange for suitable replacements.
Despite this degree of dissatisfaction, and the resultant hazardous implications, the government failed to intervene and ban the marketing of this product which was totally unsuitable and unsafe. I believe that tires marketed in Canada should be subjected to a vigorous inspection and test in order to meet Canadian road and driving conditions. After all, tires are still the basic foundation of the automobile.
This leads me to another point in respect of the claim of motor manufacturers that the

February 2, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
increased cost of new vehicles is the result of safety features. This is simply nonsense, and the manufacturers should be called upon to substantiate their claim. There is no question but that many safer instruments and devices could be installed at relatively little or no extra cost. For example, I think it would be just as cheap to manufacture a dashboard with a smooth, contoured surface as it is to have the sharp, knife-like edges we see in many models today. I think this could be incorporated without additional cost. I have known many injuries to be sustained as a result of impact against the rear view mirror, some of a minor nature but in many cases of a permanent nature.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Bigg), much improvement could be made in the construction of the bumper. The function of the bumper has been totally disregarded and it has now become an item of appeal rather than an item for safety.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Another aspect that should be investigated, and to which no reference is made in the bill or the appendix, is a minimum standard for windshield and rear window vision. This matter, naturally, could affect the total design of an automobile and indeed it should. Even today, there are many fastback models produced which have a limited amount of rear window vision and which contain detrimental blind spots. Coincidental with this, I believe it should be mandatory in Canada that all vehicles have adequate defrosting equipment in order that front, rear and side vision may not be obscured in any significant way. Naturally, this standard would probably apply to vehicles marketed in Canada only, but I think it is a matter of major importance. This has been covered adequately by other hon. members.
In looking over the 29 standards set out in the appendix to Hansard of Thursday last, I find most items to be very vague. I hope, during the consideration of the bill by the committee, we will be able to find out specifically what is meant by item 113, which is a regulation concerning hood latch systems and regulation 206 in respect of door latches, hinges and locks. These are very vague terms. I think we all realize these are basic necessities in respect of automobiles. I should like to know for the record just what provisions the automobile manufacturers must follow in this regard.
I do not wish to delay this bill unduly and, therefore, shall close by saying I believe the

bill is a necessary piece of legislation which I intend to support. I am disappointed, however, by the lack of initiative of the government in prescribing Canadian standards in addition to those set by the United States. I believe such standards are necessary. Some of the Canadian requirements have been pointed out by me and others have been pointed out by other hon. members. I refer to such things as flares and towing devices, which were mentioned by my hon. friend from Pembina.
When one reads the bill one might almost believe it had been written by the motor car companies because without standards the bill does not mean too much. In a general way, all automobile manufacturers now comply with the standards to some degree. Regardless of the safety devices installed, the effect of such devices will depend to a large degree on the driver and passengers. There can be no substitute for caution and concern. One cannot legislate judgment and courtesy on the road.
Probably the greatest single contributor to carnage on the highway today is speed. I submit that if we are really serious about curbing the mass destruction of life and property, perhaps the best and simplest way to achieve it would be to simply build an automobile which travels no more than 50 or 60 miles per hour. Then, it might not be necessary to become involved in a debate which, in many respects, is rather superficial to the basic problem. But I doubt whether such a development will ever take place. Vested interests are involved and these will continue to exist. There will also probably continue to exist a desire and a challenge, on the part of some individuals, to live dangerously. So, we will continue to hear a lot of talk about safety, new innovations and new devices after this bill is passed. We will also continue to hear the tried and proven automobile advertising theme of more power, more torque and more speed. In view of this, there can be no illusions about there being less accidents. I submit therein lies a great part of our problem of highway safety today.

Mr. Speaker, I just wish to make a few comments.
We are faced with an extremely serious problem, the problem of highway safety which must first be assured through education of those who drive vehicles and surveillance over mechanical safety of vehicles. As a matter of fact, the most advanced car, if in the hands of a careless driver, will always
February 2, 1970

result in catastrophes such as those we unfortunately see every day, especially on weekends.
It is surprising to realize that in this era of technology and progress, when vehicles can land on the moon, and a great number of mechanical problems, can be resolved with incredible accuracy, the main being living on earth, i.e. man, is forgotten and that truly improved motor vehicles that may be driven safely home yet to be devised.
Cars have been made wider, more beautiful. Sometimes, they have been made smaller, without anything being done to improve them. When you think of the $3,000, $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000 that must be payed for a car, it seems paradoxical that the safety features have been completely disregarded. Too many accidents happen on the highways for them to be all attributed to the drivers' recklessness. It is obvious that car manufacturers do not live up to their responsibilities.
I am therefore in favor of any action aimed at improving motor vehicle safety standards so as to cut down the startling number of accidents on Canadian roads.
Since the price of cars is quite high, it is quite normal for the buyer to expect something safe, something truly useful. This is why I suggest that the previous speeches were to the point. The technical aspect they dealt with must be taken into consideration, so that motor vehicles will really be made to serve the people. We do not get in a car because it likes it, but because it serves us one way or the other. Therefore, a car must be equipped with everything necessary to give us the best possible service. We must therefore think of a whole gamut of small details which are not necesarily the ones that have been thought of.
Safety belts were mentioned. It is common knowledge that practically nobody bothers about them. Sometimes accidents happen precisely because of the wearing of safety belts. There are therefore many problems, of varying importance, and we should not go to the other extreme in adding gadgets to car because this often serves no other purpose than enriching the manufacturer of these gadgets. We should therefore be concerned only with safety devices that are necessary.
I cannot be led to believe that in this century of progress, of sophistication, it is not possible to invent everything required to cut down on highway accidents through improved safety of motor vehicles.

Mr. Speaker, I want to assure you that I would not have entered the debate on this matter had it not been that I noted throughout this debate that you yourself, Sir, and those who occupy Your Honour's Chair, have allowed the discussion to involve matters such as snowmobiles and protection of aeroplanes. As I have no intention of speaking for more than about four minutes, I know without question that I will be granted the same privilege as that given to other members.
I have noted in reports over the years what it costs Canada to engage in a sea or air search and rescue when a plane goes down. It is my understanding that if a certain instrument, called a beeper, were put in a plane, hundreds of thousands of dollars would be saved in air or sea search and rescue, and also many lives might be saved.
So, I would like to recommend, on this aspect only, what I think will meet with unanimous approval, namely, that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) consider the introduction at an early date of legislation making it mandatory that all planes flying over Canada, especially private planes, be required to have this very inexpensive piece of equipment. At present our law does not require this, but I am certain that for the few hundreds of dollars it costs thousands of dollars would be saved and, in all probability, lives would also be saved. I request that this matter be taken into consideration by the Minister of Transport and that it be made compulsory for this piece of equipment to be included on all planes flying in Canada.
The second point I wish to make concerns snowmobiles. I have been doing a great deal of reading about this piece of equipment. A few years ago it was unknown, but now we have them by the thousand all across Canada. I should like to recommend to the Minister of Transport that the mechanical safety aspect of snowmobiles be included in the bill, apart from the motor vehicle aspect. However, if my reading is correct, and I have no reason to think it is not, a great many accidents are occurring on snowmobiles. I read that in our far north the snowmobile is replacing the dogs and sled. An aeroplane, with two or three passengers, might go down, necessitating air search and rescue. Similarly, a snowmobile might be lost due to an ice break, or for various other reasons, and the same air search and rescue would have to be undertak-

en. I should like to suggest that a beeper, similar to the one which I suggested should be put into planes, be put on snowmobiles or, in other words, that it be mandatory that all snowmobiles be equipped with a beeper.
I see the minister is nodding. May I point out to him that the same expenditure is involved in search and rescue operations tor a snowmobile as one undertaken for a plane. So, the point I am trying to make, however ineffectual it may be, is that it should be made mandatory that all planes in Canada or coming to Canada should be equipped with beepers, which cost only about $325 and which could save many lives. apologize to the House for being late, but I was at a committee meeting elsewhere. However, I should like to have the attention of the minister with regard to a number of points which I should like to make in relation to the bill before us. I think everyone is concerned about making a concerted attack on the whole problem of the annual slaughter on the highways, not only the thousands who are killed on the highways but the scores of thousands who are injured and the millions of dollars of damage to property which results from automobile accidents. As the minister indicated, a section of the legislation deals with the drivers' habits. The provinces have a whole litany of offences dealing with the drivers' conduct. We, ourselves, have recently amended the Criminal Code dealing with the drinking driver. Whether or not this will have a great impact, I do not know. Then, of course, the provincial departments of transport and the departments of public works are concerned with the safety of the highways. Yet we know we are spending millions of dollars annually on rebuilding, on researching, and on the question of highway safety from the point of view of the road service. Now, there remains the last one, and that has to do with the vehicle itself.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I do not care how good a highway you may have, how good a vehicle you may have, how well a driver may have been trained, if he behaves like a damned fool at the wheel all

the rest is gone for naught. There is no way in which legislation can deal with his thinking. Within limits, you can constrain him. He can drive only so fast. We have rules of the road, and laws governing such things as dangerous driving, negligence, and so forth. But there are many ways in which the mental attitude of the driver can escape any legislation.
Let us deal with Bill C-137, Mr. Speaker. I think everyone in the House wholeheartedly agrees with its objectives. These are simply an increase in the safe use of the motor vehicle, not exclusively due to the action of the driver but to the safe quality of the vehicle.
My colleague from Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Noble) spoke about his early interest in this matter. I would not want this debate to end without reminding the House, particularly many of the new members on the government side, of the efforts made by the former hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, Mr. Heward Grafftey, who at times appeared to be a lone knight in this battle. The action now being taken by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) may in large measure result from Mr. Grafftey's insistent prodding on this question. I think we all owe him a great debt of gratitude.
The bill will not guarantee against latent defects showing up in any part of a vehicle. Anything can be designed to standard, can be manufactured to standard, but this is no guarantee against a latent defect appearing in it. Further, the administration of the bill's provisions will be somewhat difficult.
As a classic example, are we going to force automobile manufacturers to design a special model for Canada? We must remember that, according to the terms of the auto pact, decisions are made as to what types of car are manufactured in Canada. The minister must know that what I have in mind here concerns winter driving conditions.
Take the example of a car designed on the fastback principle, which gives quite a low angle to the rear window. In the prairies, where the snow is drier than it is in eastern Canada, there is not much tendency for it to accumulate on such a rear window. However, in Ottawa, Montreal, New York State, and in the interior of British Columbia where the snow is much more moist, the ordinary slipstream of air passing over such a rear window is not sufficient to remove that snow. I have had this experience driving that particular type of vehicle in Ottawa. How will the ministry police such a situation? Can it

say to a manufacturer, "If that type of car is to be sold in particular regions, its design is no use"?
The other day the minister had some difficulty replying to questions about the term, "motor vehicle". He was asked what about a tractor. He replied that in certain cases a tractor might be covered by this bill, for instance if it were licensed to run on a road. But the trouble is that a manufacturer or distributor cannot determine, when he makes a sale, whether a tractor will be used primarily on the highway, or part-time on the highway, or all the time on a farm. I suggest it would be better to amend the bill to say that a motor vehicle means any vehicle except a tractor. The minister should definitely exclude tractors from the provisions of this legislation. Its seal of approval must appear on electrical and electronic apparatus, and on many other kinds of commodities. Why not require that its seal of approval be necessary for automobile components?

Narcotics Act. When this bill comes back from committee, I hope to have a lot more to say about that.

The minister says "because it is unsafe", but what if the defect were to be corrected? Say for instance there was an unsafe tie rod, and a new safer tie rod were installed, what entitlement has the Crown to seize that vehicle?
This is a matter I have continuously objected to in the drafting of statutes. Why in heaven's name do we need a cross-reference to the Fisheries Act in this bill for the provision of steps to be taken under seizure and disposal and all that sort of thing? This is just bad drafting. Perhaps the minister and his colleagues should get together and bring out a new federal seizures act, but let us not keep going back to the Fisheries Act. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should initiate a national reaserch and development program in respect of methods of proper and economic solid-waste disposal, including studies directed to the conservation of natural resources by reducing the amount of waste and unsalvageable materials and by recovery and utilization of potential resources in solid wastes; and provide technical and financial assistance to provincial and municipal governments and multi-governmental agencies in the planning, development, and conduct of solid-waste disposal programs.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
He said: Mr. Speaker, I note that although my motion was filed, if I may use that expression, since that time there has been a notice in the Citizen of January 30, about the intentions of the Province of Ontario. The headline of the article reads, "Ontario makes fresh beginning on industrial pollution controls". The body of the article reads in part:
All waste disposal sites and systems (including municipal dumps) will require provincial certificates of approval, and fines of up to $2,000 daily will be possible against violators who dispose of garbage at places and in ways not acceptable to the government.
Hamilton has a problem with regard to the disposal of solid waste emanating from the householder. I will not take up the time of the House in discussing this matter except to say that we have a secondary sewage disposal system utilized for the disposal of solid waste. I hope the federal government realizes that the people of Hamilton are concerned about this matter and are concerned because of the lack of commitment in this area by the federal government.

It can be said that as we enter the 1970's we are burying ourselves in our own waste with as little concern as we showed regarding the pollution of our waters and air. I believe it is time for us to place high on the list of priorities the question of solid-waste disposal. We must now become very concerned about smothering ourselves in the debris of our own making. I am not aware of any comprehensive statistics on the magnitude of solid-waste of all forms generated in Canada. Undoubtedly, there must be some statistics. Nevertheless, it seems to be that because of increased populations and the continuing trend towards urbanization that will be part of the pattern of the 1970's, the problem of waste, its disposal and related problems will become much more pressing than has been the case in the past.
The nature of solid-waste is variable and the problems relating to the disposal of solid-waste involve factors of geography, technology, government and public attitudes. Solid waste from industry is another source of such waste. It is of significant magnitude. Although industry is involved in the waste problem, it plays a significant role in conserving material, thus conserving raw materials, and in the recycling through the industrial process of salvaged material. For example, industrial scrap is useful in the recovery of tons of copper, lead, zinc and other metals.
The paper industry also generates annually millions of tons of waste from the production of articles utilizing paper. Waste is generated from our acceptance of items like paper packaging, paper containers, bottles and jars, plastic containers and caps, metal cans and other miscellaneous packaging materials. This indicates the magnitude of the problem in this area alone. It takes very little imagination for us to realize that society will not stop generating large quantities of this type of waste, all of which in the end has to be discarded. Waste material also results from mining
Waste Disposal Research industries and takes the form of waste rock, mill tailings, smelter slag and so on, all accumulated at mine sites. Other areas of concern, of course, are those to do with urban renewal and superhighway construction which is, to say the least, being greatly accelerated. The problem here is this: We must ask ourselves what we are to do with waste materials such as plastic, tile, metal, stones, dirt and masonry. For how long can such materials remain on site or continue to be buried?
The three divisions that must be considered when classifying waste products and their disposal problems are atmospheric, liquid and solid. Although it seems possible, it really is not practical to separate problems involving solid-waste disposal from those involving water and air pollution. For example, air pollution can be aggravated by the burning of solid wastes. Household grinding of garbage eliminates solid waste but increases liquid waste. Solid-waste disposal by means of land fill can produce problems relating to ground water supplies. Therefore, any over-all policy involving the disposal of solid wastes must be developed in association with any policy relating to liquid waste and atmospheric conditions. Accordingly, it is necessary for the federal government to adopt some unified standard. At present it seems to show no interest in this.
I think it would be very unwise for Parliament and the government to debate the Canada water bill in isolation from other factors I have mentioned because, as I said, pollution and solid-waste disposal are interrelated questions. The outpourings of households, municipalities and industry, business and agriculture in the form of waste and discarded materials bring about pollution.
The theme of my remarks is really a plea for better waste management policies and how we are to bring those into effect in order to benefit Canadians as a whole at present and in the future. We must become motivated to deal with this problem now. It matters little whether the ends of our actions are the improvement of health, the economic incentives resulting from salvaging of waste products, long range conservation programs or the removal of aesthetic insults in the form of ugly views and undesirable odours. Although we have been motivated in the past by considerations relating to health hazards, other considerations are steadfastly becoming more important.
We are mainly concerned about the following forms of waste: Organic sewage or waste
309$	COMMONS
Waste Disposal Research which is principally carried by water contained in the units we use for the disposal of our wastes; trash and garbage, by which we mean primarily the material picked up from homes, businesses and other manufacturing establishments, and automobile hulks and demolition materials. Sewage disposal units cost millions of dollars in capital, and we should determine if they offer convenient means for the collecting and transporting of solid wastes that might be collected in the systems. Substantial grants are required in the area of sewage treatment because we must encourage chemists, biochemists, microbiologists and biologists to develop innovations in the technology of sewage treatment.
I say this because it seems that professionals in this field have made scant contribution to this area.
The collection of trash and garbage is still, in many instances, carried out in a primitive way and I submit that we need to undertake studies which will examine systems of modernizing the collecting and disposal of such waste. A good many cities have no satisfactory refuse disposal system at the present time and it is not uncommon to see refuse dumped in our rivers and lakes. The complexities resulting from the disposal of waste material from various sources, the salvage aspects relating to waste material, aspects relating to water and air pollution and the logistics of transfer and disposal of wastes, create problems of great magnitude. Visual pollution by automobile hulks is becoming a matter of national concern, and immediate steps ought to be initiated to recycle scrap from old cars to our steel furnaces. In that way, we could clean up this aspect of pollution.
Programs of salvaging and reclaiming can play a very significant role in solid-waste disposal management. The re-use of scrap material can make up for any deficiency in our raw materials. Solid wastes can, therefore, be viewed, in certain instances, as resources. The recovery of these resources has been the motivation behind some salvage operations, particularly in the United States. It is vital therefore that further research be undertaken in order to determine the purposes for which such salvaged waste material can be used.
It will probably be argued, Mr. Speaker, that the problem of solid waste disposal lies in the field of urban affairs, and that the federal government has no jurisdiction for action here. It seems that the federal government is not even interested in this field. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the problem is complex and calls for co-ordination and hard

The problem of solid-waste disposal-the disposal of paper, plastics, bottles, cars, cans-has become perhaps one of the most serious problems facing the modern urban society.
The hon. member's motion is to the effect that more research should be done in this area. From what little I know of the problem,
I agree with this. I think all hon. members would agree that federal provincial, or private funds should be allocated for research if it can be shown that research in this area is necessary. The problem of course is that if we devote money to research, this money is not available for use in dealing with the problem itself. Therefore, if research is not necessary and the skills and sophistication of existing technology is sufficient, perhaps the money should be devoted to actual production and operation of the techniques which research has already given us.
I have already stated I do not intend to speak at great length on this point. Perhaps other hon. members who speak on this motion of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) will discuss it at greater length. I wish to give an example of what I have in mind, which is the East Hamilton solid-waste reduction unit which I presume is close to my hon. friend's riding. This is a large plant costing approximately $6.3 million which is now being put into operation. I understand this plant will compound solid-wastes, produce steam, and that there will be a byproduct of reclaimed minerals. According to my information, this is being done in Hamilton at perhaps no cost to the taxpayer once the capital costs are met. This is the type of project where more research is evidently not necessary but where more money is being devoted to actually dealing with the problem with the present level of technology. I am not an expert on this subject, but it appears to me that using our present technology, and without extra research, much more could be done along these lines.

I also wish to mention the program of Firestone Tire Company in dealing with old tires which now litter the countryside, waterways, roads and trash heaps. The company now has a process of reclaiming the chemical ingredients of these tires without the air pollution caused by burning them. Which has been the normal method of dealing with them up to now. I myself lived for many years in Hong Kong, which is a small island less than 30 miles long and 5 miles at its widest point. One million people live on that island, as does a population of wild deer and other wild animals. I give this as an example of proper land use and an intelligent approach to urbanization which makes it possible for a relatively small area to have wildlife as well as a very substantial and heavy human population. In that city we have an efficient waste disposal plant. Forgive me for using "we". I realize I am speaking possessively, but a number of times I have been referred to as the member for Hong Kong. But to return to my subject, a by-product of this plant is building materials, such as building blocks. The costs of building and operating this plant are not met by the sale of building blocks. There is a certain deficit which has to be made up. Nevertheless, it has been possible to substantially meet the cost of solid-waste disposal by the sale of these by-products. This is the type of operation which Canadians should study.
