Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) on this motion. It is a very good one. I am sure it is the precursor of many efforts that will follow from many quarters to focus on a problem that is increasingly recognized as being of major importance.
The hon. member's motion has roughly two arms to it. One calls for research and asks the federal government to initiate research into solid-waste disposal to reduce its volume, and to look into methods of recovery and use of such materials that are beneficial. The second arm of the motion calls for technical and financial assistance to the provinces and to municipal governments-he even goes so far as to include multi-government agencies- for planning, developing and continuing programs.
Waste Disposal Research
The hon. member in moving his motion very properly recognizes that this is an urban problem. It is a problem of concentrations of population in relatively small areas. It is a problem of an increasingly affluent society. The beer cans and discarded, used automobiles that litter our highways and provide eyesores are the by-products of a society whose members have two cars in the garage, two television sets in the home and an increasingly high standard of living-a society that places high value on labour services yet neglects the elements of recovery that are essential if we are to reduce this problem to manageable proportions.
Every year in Canada some 400,000 automobiles are scrapped. A disturbingly small proportion of them are scrapped through the established channels through which full recovery of their materials is possible. Approximately 19 million to 20 million tons per year of solid wastes are, as estimated by one authority, being produced in our urban centres. Within the last ten years this amount has increased by 10 per cent in the country of our neighbour to the south, according to our best estimates, and will continue to increase. We are told that roughly Impounds per day of municipal solid waste per person is produced. It is estimated by one authority that in 1980 this will go up to 5 J pounds per person.
In the United States, every person uses per year 250 metal cans, 135 bottles, 338 metal and plastic caps and 6 tubes, including four tubes of toothpaste. These are just a few indicators of the mountains of surplus materials that are being discharged from our increasingly urban communities. The mover of the motion said we are literally burying ourselves in our own wastes. This has been said many times. This is in fact an urban problem. Those of us who have served on municipal councils know how urban it is and how the nature of the problem has changed. A decade ago ashes were an important part of this problem. Now, thanks to the change to heating oils and natural gas, ashes are an almost negligible part of wastes.
We now have an increasing proportion of brush from suburbanites who have their own gardens and have to discharge their own materials because they are forbidden to burn it in their own backyards because it would pollute the air. We have increasing proportions of industrial wastes. We have in Canada, I am sure, the highest proportion of newsprint and cardboard waste per capita.
3100	COMMONS
Waste Disposal Research This is perhaps a doubtful feature of this magnificent resource of our country which has led to its rather reckless use.
Convenient containers, methods of packaging, and trends in public health which insist that everything be covered and nothing be left in such a way that it can be contaminated in the process of distribution, have contributed to the waste disposal problem. The problem has to be viewed in its entirety, and it has to be analyzed at various stages.
The definition of solid waste is fairly arbitrary as between liquid, solid and atmospheric waste. As the mover of the motion pointed out, the one embraces the other; measures to control atmospheric pollution where there are particles involved will often accentuate the solid disposal problem. Liquid and solid wastes are in many cases interchangeable. Let us consider the situation where the woman of the house has a garbage disposal unit which chops the garbage to shreds. It simply converts solid waste to a liquid form of waste, and there is a problem at a different point. The collection of waste, its processing and disposal must be attacked at every stage.
There is also a major secondary materials industry. It is estimated that something like $5 billion to $10 billion worth of waste could be recovered in the United States. The recovery of scrap copper could amount to 80 per cent of the new copper used in the United States. The recovery of lead from secondary materials and scrap is equal to twice the domestic lead production in the United States. The recovery of materials such as paper, rubber, plastic, textiles, even hair and feathers, and in some cases precious metals, has an economic base. A community that has sufficient incentive and interest in that base could build up an industry.
This affluent society of ours increasingly destroys the economic base of the secondary materials industry. How does it do so? It does so by its social attitudes. Anyone engaged in the business of recovering waste is associated with the junk collector. Collection and transfer points are zoned out of existence by municipal authorities. There is no positive encouragement to make such collection points comply with sanitary requirements. There are no research programs initiated to establish a means by which these places could be made acceptable to communities. The approach of our affluent society is just to zone them out of existence.
In our society we are very fortunate that the standard of living and wage rates are as

DEBATES	February 2. 1970
high as they are, and I would not in any way want to change them. However the high cost of living defeats the secondary recovery process because the high cost of labour makes the cost of recovery prohibitive. We have frequently criticized local government because it is completely self-defeating as far as orderly waste recovery programs are concerned. Garbage collection in its rough sense, in broad population usage, tends to be fragmented over different municipalities. This is one of the services that is frequently left, in a two-tier system of municipal government, at the primary level and is not transferred to the regional level.
Regional authorities may have control of waste disposal sites because these are so few, and expensive. The fragmented nature of municipal government, each with its own zoning laws, each with its own by-laws governing the collection and disposal of waste, and each with its own system, makes this a very difficult matter. Municipalities may farm out the job to private contractors. They may have a municipal operation. The effect of such a state of affairs is to make almost impossible an orderly arrangement for the secondary materials industry, with sufficient inducement to engage in planning and investment in capital facilities, collection facilities and transfer points. This is almost entirely due to the fragmented nature of local government in our big city areas.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I served on a municipal council in this city. Every second year we had the problem of how to acquire a satisfactory land-fill site: that was the language used. I am sure hon. members of this House would be astonished to know how many parts of the city of Ottawa have been built up by the sanitary land-fill method. Within my own recollection some of the best parkways along the Rideau River have had five or six feet of sanitary land-fill dumped there. It has been dumped on both sides of the Rideau River parkway and on the Ottawa River parkway.
A major sand re-fill operation took place on the Ottawa River parkway in the Britannia area, in my own constituency. The problem, of course, is very simple: Sites become more difficult to find. Every year the cost of haulage to sites farther and farther removed from the point of origin of the solid waste becomes more prohibitive in an economic sense. More and more communities regard the temporary land-fill operation as a community nuisance that must be stopped at all costs.

The municipality, generally speaking, has two choices. It can incinerate and pollute the air, or it can engage in landfill operations, face the violent objection of residents of the area and run the serious risk of polluting the water and destroying the natural marshes and other features which are part of the environment for a considerable time to come. Last but not least, they must face the fact that the sites that are reasonably available within economic hauling distance are rapidly being exhausted.
The hon. member for Hamiltion West commented favourably, I gather, on the announcement by the government of Ontario that it intends to licence disposal sites and impose penalties on people who do not use proper disposal sites. I believe this is action on the negative side, the penalty side, and is not proper use of the jurisdiction the province has in this area. I do not wish to hide behind the jurisdictional problem. I am one who believes the federal government also should take a great deal of initiative. It is easy to do just what the province of Ontario has done. It is just one small part of the story, that is, placing a prohibition without giving any answers to dealing with the problem. I see the hon. member agrees with me.

I should be very happy to hear the hon. member's view if he disagrees, because I know the type of problem the municipalities face. They have to face the fact that these sites are not available any more. What can be done? A prohibition can be placed on dumping. Then, where does the garbage and solid waste go? This is not exclusively a problem of the federal government, as much as I would like the federal government to have authority over it. I think it is a serious enough matter that when we have a federal-provincial conference on urban problems, it should receive high priority on the agenda. There is no way in which one level of government can cope with this problem. Of all the problems- in the whole area of urban affairs, this one has an extremely local content, a regional content
Waste Disposal Research and a national content. By the very nature of things I believe the development of a national program would have to be part of a co-operative endeavour at all levels of government.
I should like to say a word or two about the problem of automobiles. Like any other member of this House, when I take a drive on Sunday afternoon out into the country, especially in the winter when the leaves are not there to hide the view, I see the hulks of wrecked automobiles. There is no question that this is an unpleasant sight and that something must be done about it. The National Capital Commission spends in the order of $20,000 each year in hauling away abandoned automobiles from the green belt area. This is just one community and one area. When the owner of an automobile decides it is no longer worth driving, or decides he can no longer drive it, he hauls it out at night, takes off the licence plates, hopes he has succeeded in obliterating the identifying marks, and abandons it. This has become a great problem in areas such as Detroit and New York.
I have read of proposals whereby governments could deal with the problem of abandoned automobiles. I have spoken to people who know something about the automobile business. When I ask what can be done with an old automobile, I am told that first it is stripped. Certain parts of a salvageable nature are removed, such as the battery which has recoverable lead, the tires which have recoverable rubber, and other items. Then the automobile is taken somewhere and burned. By burning, it is reduced to metallic remains; then the burned hulk can be compressed and has an economic salvage value.
Part of the difficulty is what has happened in respect of the steel industry. The steel industry does not need a large volume of scrap material any more. There was a time in the steel industry, about 15 years ago, when scrap metal was a very important item, but because of recent developments the requirements for scrap has been reduced. This has had a most unfortunate effect on the removal of automobiles from our landscape.
The hon. member said that site control is needed. I quite agree. I wonder what other measures might be taken to cope with this problem. I understand the Japanese have developed a good method of recovering automobiles, but in a country like ours the recovery of automobiles is not a simple matter. There must be recovery points, and we have long distances to deal with and
3102	COMMONS
Waste Disposal Research sparse population. We must recognize that a recovery method based on burning would involve pollution of the air. We must have some disposal method whereby we can reduce the extraneous materials which pollute the air.
I believe, also, we must have a method of subsidy in respect of bringing the material into a central point. The tragedy of a solid-waste disposal program is that it has such a precarious economic base because of the attitude toward it, the trends in our society, the cost factor and everything else. It seems to me we cannot reply upon a "do nothing" attitude to develop positive salvage and secondary material recovery industries. The industry will have to receive a good deal of assistance and research. It will have to receive a good deal of help by way of subsidy and help from local authorities who will have to adapt their zoning and regional planning requirements at certain central points to which waste should be attracted and where it can be recovered.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This program will call for a national code of waste removal which, in my opinion, can be developed only by co-operative action at the three levels of government in Canada. I look forward to the day in the near future when, at a conference called to discuss urban affairs, this problem will receive high priority and will lead to the kind of measures which were mentioned in the debate today.

Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) began this debate last week he said that this was one of the most important pieces of legislation with which Parliament would be concerned this session. When 1 looked at my file, which holds reports covering only a small fraction of the problems concerning automobile safety, 1 realized the minister had not exaggerated. If anything, he underplayed the seriousness of the problem.
Today I called the National Safety Council in order to get its most recent figures on deaths, injuries and property damage caused by automobile accidents. The most recent figures cover 1967 and 1968. The figures for 1969 are not yet at hand, but I am sure they will not show any drastic reduction. According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, 5,412 people died as a result of automobile accidents in 1967, 165,000 people were injured, and there were over 330,000 claims for property damage. The estimate of property damage in that year as a result of automobile accidents was in the neighbourhood of $650 million. In 1968 there was a slight reduction in the number of deaths caused by automobile accidents. In that year the figure was 5,375, but the number of people injured increased to 172,718. The number of claims for property damage rose to 360,000.
It is because of this kind of situation that finally in 1970, in both Canada and the United States, we are beginning to enact legislation which, if enforced, will cut the toll of deaths, injuries and property damage caused by car accidents. And if we are doing this in 1970 it is because a few individuals in the United States, one or two in Canada, and a few organizations put the spotlight of publicity on defects found in cars over the last 15 or 20 years.
In this situation the role of the automobile companies in Canada has been a disgraceful one, a despicable one. Mr. Speaker, let us face the facts. Automobile companies in Canada are 98 per cent controlled by the automobile companies in the United States, and from the

beginning they have rejected the idea that there was anything basically wrong with their product.
Automobile companies tried to convince the public that automobile accidents were caused by improper driving habits or by defects in roads. Of course, some automobile accidents have resulted from those causes. But the automobile companies also tried to convey the idea that there was nothing wrong with automobiles themselves or, if there was, the companies had done everything possible to correct the defects.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure members of this House know that the person most responsible for publicizing the completely uncaring attitude and negligence of the automobile companies was Ralph Nader in the United States. I am sure that members of this House will know, too, that when Ralph Nader's arguments began to have an impact on the United States public, General Motors, the biggest automobile company in the world, or their lawyers, hired investigators to undertake detailed research into Ralph Nader's private life. Mr. Nader did this work in the United States. Canadian auto safety standards will, in effect, be set in Washington where there has been, and still is, consistent opposition by the automobile industry which has so far frustrated genuine efforts in this field. The United States government has tended to accept standards set by the industry.
I am afraid that in adopting similar standards-the 29 points which will be dealt with by regulation later-we will in effect be adopting the United States standards which have consistently proven to be completely inadequate. Besides that, I presume the safety features required for Canada's climate, such as rear-window defrosters, will not be included because they are not necessary in a large part of the United States; therefore, neither the government nor the auto companies will make them a standard feature of United States automobile manufacturers.
Even if this is true of the United States, it certainly is not true of Canada and we should make it a requirement of new car manufacture that rear-window defrosters are included. I drive a Swedish car, a Volvo, which has

a rear-window defroster, and I can tell the minister that it works very effectively even in the Ottawa winter. A clear rear-window makes it possible for me to be a better and safer driver. I hope this feature will be included in the Canadian legislation. In effect, the legislation is meaningless unless Canadian auto safety standards are specifically spelled out.
Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago I said that the United States automobile companies have been conspicuous by their refusal not only to take the lead in promoting safer automobiles but in their opposition to anybody else getting involved in this field. In hearings before a U.S. Senate subcommittee a few years ago headed by Senator Philip Hart, Senator Edward Kennedy was questioning the president of General Motors. He inquired how much profit General Motors had made in the year before the hearings. After some protest it was admitted that in the last fiscal year General Motors had made $1,500 million profit. When Senator Kennedy pressed a question to elicit how much had been spent in research for automobile safety, the president of General Motors had to admit that the figure was less than $5 million. As Senator Kennedy pointed out, that was less than one-twentieth of one per cent of their profit.
When people like Ralph Nader bring to the attention of the public the research findings of engineers and medical scientists at universities such as Cornell, Harvard, California, Minnesota and institutions such as the Liberty Mutual Insurance Company, and John F. Gordon, the president of General Motors, ridicules amateur engineers for trying to take over responsibilities that belong to competent engineers in the industry, it makes one stop and think.
Indeed, the only honest thing Mr. Gordon said was that the responsibility lay with the engineers of the industry but, in fact, the industry had completely abdicated its responsibility. The institutions which I have mentioned, Cornell, Harvard, California and Minnesota, uncovered auto designs which led to 40,000 fatalities per year in the United States at that time. They found that cars were likely to have doors pop open when there was an accident, had cardboard-like roof structures, uprootable seats, flying cushions, flying metal dash-knobs, chisel-like rear-view mirrors, and above all dangerous parts of the steering wheel. These were just a few of the 100-odd design defects found by the research engineers.

The United States Optometric Foundation performed a series of studies, and the projects director, Dr. Merrill J. Allen, reported:
Not a single car provides a suitable visual environment for daytime driving.
Similarly, a Cornell group established substantial variations in the strength of door-latches among various makes, but all were below minimum adequate safety regulations. The Liberty Mutual Insurance Company in the United States some years ago arranged for the construction of what they called safe survival cars. The company took four standard 1960 Chevrolets, removed the gingerbread, the chrome geegaws and unsafe features, and replaced them with dozens of safety improvements that would have added not more than $10 to the cost of production. Among those improvements were collapsible steering assemblies, automatic fire protection systems, roll bars to strengthen roofs and safety braking devices.
Every one of these safety features has been known to Detroit for years. Detroit engineers have known for years that impacts against steering columns are responsible for a large percentage of serious injury-producing accidents and deaths. But when it was suggested to General Motors that collapsible steering wheel assemblies should be built into General Motors cars, the company said that was not practical. However, one year later when the heat was turned on by the Senate investigating committee, lo and behold, the company installed collapsible steering wheel assemblies in certain cars as an optional feature. Now, a few years later, after considerable pressure by those who are really interested in automobile safety, collapsible steering assemblies are to be made part of an automobile's standard equipment.
It is interesting to note that automobile companies are more concerned about the appearance of cars, because that is important from the point of view of selling them. You change the appearance when you want to introduce a new model. But safety features which protect the lives and well-being of passengers have been made available only very recently as optional features for which the purchaser has to pay more money. It has been demonstrated conclusively that automobile companies have not cared about safety because in their opinion safety features do not sell cars. At hearings in 1965, General

Motors chairman, Frederic Donner, said that the-
-decision to offer an item as optional equipment recognizes what I believe is the basic freedom of the customer to pay the cost of tailoring a car to his own specifications or rejecting whatever he may not want.
In other words, if the customer wants a safety feature, he must pay for it. I have already said that styling will sell a car, but apparently safety features will not. Similarly, faulty tires have been responsible for a substantial percentage of automobile accidents and fatalities. In 1965 John Floberg, secretary and general counsel of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, made this comment at the end of the hearings before the United States subcommittee:
I submit that the best standard, the time-tested and proved standard and the appropriate free enterprise standard of quality should be the one that has in the case of tires, as in the case of other consumer products, worked most satisfactorily; namely, the discriminating and sophisticated taste of the American consumer.
Senator Gaylord Nelson of Wisconsin has introduced several bills covering tire standards. I will refer to them soon. It became obvious during Congressional hearings that the consumer really could not choose because he was never given information on which to base his choice; therefore, he could make no meaningful choice when it came to tires. I wish to refer to some of Senator Nelson's discoveries, because I think we realize that what applies to cars in the United States also applies to cars in Canada; defects in United States cars become apparent in Canadian cars and measures that will make cars safe in the United States are also applicable in Canada. Among several comments that Senator Nelson made on February 23, 1965, are the following, as reported in the Congressional Record. It is significant that only now, almost five years later, are we in this country and in the United States beginning to consider legislation in this field. The report I have in my hand reads in part as follows:
If cars were built so that protection could be provided for the head alone, at least one out of five people who are now dying in auto accidents would be saved.
If cars were built with seat and shoulder belts which would hold people in the car in an accident, thousands of lives would be saved: If a person is thrown from the car, the chance of death is five times as great.
If cars were built with only three basic changes, occupants could probably survive any crash up to 35 miles per hour-and statistics show that 87 per cent of all accidents occur at impact speed of 35

miles per hour or below. The three basic changes are: shoulder harnesses; doors which will stay closed in a crash; and collapsible steering shafts

The need for changes is obvious. But one factor impedes progress in this area. That factor is the conviction in Detroit that 'safety doesn't sell.' It is the stylist who reigns supreme in the automobile industry, not the safety and engineering experts.
Senator Nelson advocated the following safety features on motor vehicles: collapsible steering wheels, shoulder harness safety-belt anchors, specific types of safety glass, smog removing exhaust systems, standardized transmission controls to avoid confusion, and uniform bumper heights. We used to think that bumpers were designed to protect cars from damage in accidents, but if one looks at a car one will notice that they are becoming fancier and fancier and will only hurt a person or a car coming into contact with them. The automobile companies are making bumpers like that because they are not so much interested in safety as in the look of the car.
In 1966 Senator Nelson began to press for a bill to set tire standards. It would have given the consumer some protection against faulty tires. Disturbing stories came to light in the inquiries he conducted and the evidence submitted. The following was found:
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
That many new automobiles are being sold with tires which are designed to carry the normal load for which the automobile was designed.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this still applies. It was also found:
That size labels on tires-the only basis a motorist has for determining load capacity-were never meant to indicate the precise size. An 8.00 by 14 tire, which official tables indicate should carry an 1,180-pound load, may actually be smaller than a 7.50 by 14 tire, which is supposed to carry only 1,090 pounds.
That quality labels on tires, such as deluxe, premium, and first-line, have no meaning whatever and "there is no way to tell one tire grade from another."
Senator Nelson reported that he wrote to the presidents of the four major automobile manufacturing firms to ask them directly whether the tires supplied with their new cars were adequate to carry the loads for which the cars were designed. Not one of them replied with an unqualified yes.
American Motors replied that its cars could safely carry a full load, provided-
I think this should be noted.
[DOT]-the tires were specially inflated.
General Motors stated that the design guide in selecting tires was three passengers, but that its sedans could safely carry six passengers plus 200
February 2, 1970

pounds of luggage, provided the tires were specially inflated.
Chrysler said simply that its tires were adequate "provided they are properly maintained."
Ford Motor Co. said that it has been customary to make tire selections on the basis of a three-passenger load. But Ford said its sedans could carry six passengers plus luggage if the tires were specially inflated.
This was the testimony they gave Senator Nelson. Consumers who purchased the cars were never told that special measures were required tor inflating the tires. In other words, consumers had no way of knowing whether the tires they were purchasing were of adequate quality to give them the protection they needed.
I do not have time to put it on the record this evening, but Senator Nelson was able to document hundreds of cases where cars with new tires which had been used for less than
1,000	or 2,000 miles had been involved in serous accidents because the tires collapsed. Why? It was not because they were necessarily inadequately built, but because the people operating the cars had not been given the information that the tires simply could not carry the load which they expected them to carry. I refer to sedans and station wagons that people use to take their families on camping trips, etc. This was the record in 1965 and 1966, and it has not really changed. In November, 1968, Ralph Nader was able to publicize a partially completed study by the Federal Trade Commission staff in the United States which said:
-U.S. auto dealers and manufacturers have not lived up to guarantees they give on new cars-
The study says that auto industry "quality control . .. has apparently yielded under the pressure to produce more cars."
It said warranties are designed primarily to help sell cars and have not resulted in improved quality or service.
The report further stated:
"The failure of the warranty to provide new car buyers with substantially defect-free cars ... results from slack quality control at the manufacturer's level, combined with soaring car sales of dealers, shortages of skilled mechanics and inadequate allowance to dealers for pre-delivery inspection."
We know that since Mr. Nader and others began publicizing the defects in cars, the car manufacturers have finally realized that when they discover a number of cars, sometimes hundreds, thousands or tens of thousands, have defects they should not do as they did until a couple of years ago; I refer to their very quietly informing the dealers that there
Motor Vehicle Safety
was something wrong with the Buick, Cadillac, Chrysler or Ford. In an almost surreptitious manner the dealer would then get in touch with the purchaser and try to persuade him to bring his car in to be checked, to see if the defect was as serious as the manufacturer thought it was. The manufacturers now make regular public announcements when defects are discovered. This was not done for a long time. They scoffed when Ralph Nader and Heward Grafftey publicized the built-in defects in Canadian and United States cars. Public attention forced the automobile companies to make these announcements.
This is the record of the North American automobile manufacturers. It is a record of refusal to face up to their responsibilities, one of refusing to spend money on research to make automobiles safe. As I mentioned earlier, research has been left to universities and non-profit organizations. Publicity has been carried out by organizations such as the Consumers' Union in the United States. The automobile companies have dragged their feet.
I am worried about two aspects of this bill. I am worried that the standards the minister will be working with, and the regulations which will be drafted to cover the 29 points which he proposes to bring under review by means of this bill, are to a large extent those which have been agreed by the United States auto manufacturers. I submit this is not good enough.
I submit that the government should be prepared to establish a research and testing organization financed by it. I feel this should be undertaken by the government in co-operation with one or more Canadian universities to carry out scientific and objective research and testing of automobiles. We should not leave it, as we have in the past, to the automobile companies. As the record proves very conclusively, they are completely disinterested. They have done as little as possible. I submit that the leopard has not changed its spots; it is the same leopard. They will do no more than they are forced to by the government and by public opinion.
The second major reservation I have about this legislation is, what will happen after it is passed? Who will police the legislation? Who will ensure that the automobile companies live up to the specifications and regulations drafted by the government? I am concerned about the hesitancy of this government and the government of the United States to act. I

am concerned about the desire of this government to pare the budget and reduce the number of civil servants. I am concerned because even though there will be legislation and laws will be passed, there will be little, if any, enforcement of the regulations and therefore little, if any, inducement for the automobile companies to live up to the rules and regulations which will be enacted.
If the minister means business, and if the government wants to protect the Canadian people, it will not be enough to simply pass this law. It will not be enough for the department simply to draft regulations and to get an order in council proclaiming them. A very effective agency, with sufficient staff will be required to police the automobile companies to ensure that they do what up until now they have not been prepared to do, that is, build cars which are safe, cars which the people of Canada can drive with reasonable assurance that they are as safe as can be built. Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in this debate because many of the ramifications of Bill C-137 find a focal point in my constituency of Halton. This bill affects the actual lives of people, and this very month hundreds of Canadian citizens will become victims of accidents involving automobiles.
Transversing Halton are two of the busiest highways in Canada and, indeed, on this continent. I refer to the Queen Elizabeth Way and the Macdonald-Cartier Freeway. Literally tens of thousands of automobiles and other vehicles use these highways each day. Hardly a day passes when someone is not brought into our hospitals because of an accident due to drivers who may be careless or unthinking, or whose vehicles may be mechanically defective. Although this bill cannot and does not attempt to regulate highway traffic, it is nevertheless encouraging to know that the minister, in introducing Bill C-137, indicated that his department is co-operating with the provinces to improve safety standards in connection with highway traffic throughout Canada.
In Halton we have one of Canada's largest automobile and truck manufacturers, Ford of

Canada. Their standards of practice and their attitudes toward measures of safety are of vital concern to practically every Canadian. The Canadian automotive companies producing north American-type cars and trucks have for the past two model years been complying voluntarily with United States federal safety standards legislation. This has been done primarily because of the Canada-U.S. automotive trade pact which allows free passage of automotive vehicles and parts across the Canada-U.S. border.
It follows that when cars are being produced in both countries for sale in both countries, it is most efficient and economic to have them identical. This leads up to the desire of all Canadian automotive companies that the standards be identical with those now in force in the United States. Any variation would lead to horrendous problems in the manufacturing area and would, in effect, work against the program as contained in the auto pact. Any deviation would also result in higher manufacturing costs which undoubtedly would be passed on, at least in part, to the consumer.
I think the minister is moving in the right direction at this point by having the first list, as contained in this bill, conform to the American safety standards. However, this should not be another area in which it might be said we are being dictated to by forces outside our country. I believe that we in Canada can show leadership in the field of automotive safety. I would strongly urge the minister and his department to enlist the cooperation of those organizations and individuals who are concerned with the safety of our people when they venture out onto our highways.
We have the people in Canada who, through their observations and experience, have the knowledge to tell us what can be done. We also have the people who know what can be done. This latter group would involve the automobile manufacturers. I understand they are already working with the Department of Transport to develop better standards. Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the debate on this bill, and have read a number of the speeches made by hon. members. It is a measure that is of great interest not only to members of this House but to all the citizens of our nation who are well acquainted with motor vehicles and with the hazards associated with those vehicles. Most facets of safety have already been covered by hon. members and it is not my intention to go over all the points again. However, I feel I should briefly outline several points that in my opinion should be considered hand-inhand with the present regulations and with the provisions outlined in this measure.
I feel that in dealing with the problem of highway safety there must be full co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal levels of government. Sound, sensible and enforcible safety measures must be enacted and enforced by every level of government. Only in this way can we cut down appreciably the tragic number of motor vehicle accidents which occur every year.
For year there has been need for a national automotive safety code. It is amazing that something more concrete was not done about it prior to 1970. Car safety has now become a No. 1 health problem in Canada. I believe it can be called a health problem. The large number of people who are killed and crippled on our highways makes it a national disgrace. Many accidents could have been avoided, and the intensity of injuries lessened, had a national automotive safety code been established years ago.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
As we look back on our laws and regulations it is an amazing and remarkable fact that our government protects our food, pro-21611-581
Motor Vehicle Safety
tects our water to a degree, especially drinking water, protects other aspects of health; we have building codes to make sure that our housing is up to standard, we have standards for electrical wiring, and a large number of other protective measures are taken to look after our citizens; but for years we have neglected one of the greatest causes of death and injury to Canadians, that is, the modern automobile. I believe that is why the bill before us has given rise to so much interest among hon. members and, I am quite sure, among the general public. Improvements in this field are being made and a measure of government action, both federal and provincial, is being taken. However, we have still a long way to go to cover all the points which we should be covering.
There are two or three aspects of traffic safety which I should like to cover very briefly and point out that in my opinion they must go hand in hand with the various codes which we are trying to establish in this piece of legislation. The three aspects of traffic safety which complement legislation of this type deal first with the drivers of automobiles, second with highway design, and third with the safety features of vehicles which automobile manufacturing firms and governments have neglected for generations.
In so far as training of drivers is concerned, I am not putting all the blame on the deferral government because much of the responsibility is provincial. It is the provinces which have the licensing of automobiles under their jurisdiction. We have driver training programs in schools in various provinces of this nation. In my opinion the training of drivers should be undertaken by schools all across Canada. I have heard people say that this type of training does not necessarily result in a decrease of traffic accidents. This is just not so. Training of drivers must complement legislation of the type we have before us. This is why I urge full co-operation among federal, provincial and municipal governments to ensure that this type of training is made available to the young people of this nation who are the future drivers of vehicles and who, according to statistics, are involved in the greatest number of accidents.
I urge that the federal government approach the provincial governments which have not proceeded with this program. I urge hon. members to help ensure that this type of driver training is undertaken by schools all across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, so that when our young people get behind

February 2, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
the wheel ol a car they know what hazards and dangers they are likely to face on the highway.
Another action1 which should be taken by the government and which should complement this legislation is research. I am referring now to research in highway design. I think that too much is left to chance at present. I realize that every highway department has a group of very competent engineers who work on highway design; but as we get more powerful vehicles and as the average speed of our cars gradually increases, there is more need than ever for the federal and provincial governments to enter into research of highway design in co-operation with each other. I believe that if this were done, a great number of accidents which presently take place would be eliminated. I suggest that this is a field into which the federal government should enter, and it should support, at least financially, research programs which are desperately needed.
The third point which I wish to make has already been covered by speakers on all sides of the House. It concerns vehicle safety. Other speakers have said, and I say it again, that we are very fond of putting flashy chrome on our cars. The manufacturers of automobiles know that automobile owners everywhere in the world are real suckers for something that looks flashy. They have neglected-there is absolutely no doubt about it, so I will not go into all the details again-many safety features which should be incorporated into motor vehicles before they are allowed on the highways of this nation.
I will give the House one example-the height and quality of bumpers. On many of our vehicles bumpers are placed at different heights. The statistics which are available to individuals who wish to obtain them indicate that a number of injuries and deaths could have been avoided if the height of bumpers had been standardized. Also, the quality of bumpers should be improved because most bumpers would be dented if they hit a package of popcorn.
This is an area in which we need a safety council and a government which will check on the facts and then insist firmly that this type of safety feature be incorporated into vehicles. We can still get good design in a car and a vehicle that will operate efficiently, without losing any of its effectiveness, with many more safety features incorporated into it than we have today.

There is one more aspect of vehicle safety which I will mention very briefly. I refer to testing. I believe that motor vehicles should have compulsory testing in Canada. After you have had a motor vehicle for a period of time, you should be forced to have it tested at a proper testing station by competent mechanics. There are motor vehicles being driven around Ottawa and, in fact, in every city in Canada that have no right to be on the highways of this nation. What are we doing about it? The neglect is nationwide for the simple reason that compulsory testing has not been introduced in every province. One or two of the provinces may have this requirement.
I know that two or three years ago we had some interesting information from the city of Vancouver which had introduced compulsory testing of motor vehicles. The number of accidents caused by faulty mechanism was very low compared with the number of accidents in the provinces in which there was not compulsory testing.
I am convinced that the older a vehicle gets, the more chance there is of the vehicle breaking down. That is why we need this type of testing. We are not trying to put the driver of an automobile in a strait jacket by saying that he must do this, that or the other thing; but a driver who is on a public highway should realize that it is his duty, not only to protect himself but to protect other drivers on that highway.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
An individual can have an up-to-date automobile in top-notch shape, and yet can have his family wiped out because the vehicle belonging to another driver had not been properly checked for defects. I have no hesitation in urging most strongly that the testing of motor vehicles should be part and parcel of the safety code from one end of Canada to the other.
A previous speaker mentioned the standardization of signs. I should like to say a few words on this subject. Thank goodness it is coming, because signs should be standardized. When I cross the bridge into Quebec, or go to any other province, I should know that I will be driving on highways in exactly the same situation as I would in my native province of British Columbia. This is just common sense, Mr. Speaker. Signs should be standardized throughout the North American continent.

As legislators we must do our best to obtain the type of safety measures which will protect the ever-increasing travelling public in Canada.

There are only three or four general comments I should like to make in winding up this debate. It will become evident in committee that the effectiveness of this measure will to large degree depend upon the kind of cooperation we can achieve with the provinces. For this reason I have worked with the appropriate ministers in the provinces from the outset to ensure that companion legislation is introduced at the provincial level so we will have a measure that will go beyond the competence of the federal government in defining what is a safe car, or a reasonably safe car at the time it leaves the factory.
Once it gets into the provinces, replacement parts, new tires and various things of this kind, and the matter of testing, are within provincial jurisdiction. I believe we have established the most effective level of cooperation and an awareness on the part of both levels of government of the need for co-operation. 1 am sure this will produce the desired result.
Motor Vehicle Safety
From the beginning I have been concerned with what might be described as off-highway vehicles, namely, snowmobiles, and have wondered how we might come up with an effective nationwide set of standards. Under his legislation I am satisfied that we have the competence to introduce safety standards so far as the new vehicle is concerned. We have had discussions with the provinces to see if we cannot arrive at some sort of standards on licensing, because in some instances snowmobiles are permitted to cross highways and in other instances they are not licensed at all. In other cases they are licensed to travel on the shoulder of the highway. While agreeing completely with hon. members who feel there is a need for regulation in this field, I believe we have to get the various jurisdictions to agree on a set of standards and then introduce as many of them as possible into the new vehicle.
I was most impressed with the comments of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who talked about the need for some kind of homing device and coupled this with reference to the need for a similar mechanism on aircraft. Even knowing your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to drift too far from the subject, but I still do not understand why this is not part of the mechanism of aircraft. I have received submissions from various aviation clubs and the like, and I find myself in complete agreement with the hon. member that this device seems thoroughly logical in terms of aircraft. I have asked if there is good reason why we should not have it, otherwise it would be my intention to bring in this type of legislation.
As far as surface vehicles are concerned, we may have to make some distinctions because there is a difference between a vehicle being used for pleasure in the immediate vicinity of the home and one being employed for commercial or transportation purposes in the north. I undertake to see whether there is any kind of homing device that might be used in this way. There is no doubt that search and rescue is a costly business as far as governments are concerned, but it is tragic that sometimes lives are lost when people are only a few miles from the rescue party because there is no means of locating them.
There were many other interesting and constructive comments during the debate. The only point that I felt was not emphasized as much as I would have expected was my reference to the role of research into causes of accidents. As we have said repeatedly, and

February 2, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
members opposite also commented on it, you can build the safest automobile in the world, but if it hits a child, the child is probably maimed or killed. No matter how safe the automobile is, if it topples over an embankment and rolls 50, 60 or 100 feet, the risk is very great. Apart from making the car as safe as possible, we must try to find the scientific reason for so many accidents happening. Ruling out the impaired driver, there is still a surprisingly large volume of accidents caused by apparently normal people not driving at excessive rates of speed. But there seems to be very little interest in research into this area.
A related question is highway design and its affect on accidents. I believe the research and development section of the Department of Transport can be of considerable help to the provinces in trying to determine, not merely standards of size but to see if we cannot recommend standards on a nationwide basis to reduce many of the problems and make the roads safer.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe this bill will help us considerably, but I would ask that members not lay too much emphasis on the 29 standards. They happen to be the ones in existence at the present time, but if anyone comes up with other improvements we will be more than glad to introduce them once they have been tested. I suggest this is only a small part of the problem. If we are to attack the problem as effectively as I believe we can, we must consider the driver, the causes of accidents and also the "ways" system-if we can use that expression-that is, the highway itself.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
In any event, I still consider this an historic piece of legislation. I believe if we bring it before the committee shortly we can provide the kinds of answers for which hon. members are looking. I for one look forward to bringing the bill back to the House and completing a progressive move forward for the people of Canada. I thank all hon. members for their help.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

(Mr. Jamieson.]
That the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, in consultation with Mr. Speaker, be directed to study the question of radio and television broadcasting of the proceedings of the House and its committees, including the legal, procedural, and technical aspects thereof, and the question of arrangements made for reporters for the electronic media in the Parliament Buildings.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will not take much of the time of the House in speaking on this matter. May I indicate that in the English version of the motion there is typographical error. The printed words on the second line reading, "ratio and television broadcasting", should read "radio and television broadcasting." I think a comparison with the French language version will confirm that this is so.
Perhaps I ought to refer the House, as the most effective way of dealing with this matter, to the debate which took place some ten months ago on March 26, 1969, when the question of having a committee to study the broadcasting of the proceedings of the House was being considered. At that time I said, as reported at page 7164 of Hansard:
Thereafter, I expect that the house will want to ask the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization to make a preliminary study of the question of working out appropriate procedures for broadcasting in the House. I repeat, however, that I believe we should let the committee complete the work we have given it.
At that time I suggested it would be desirable to let the committee consider procedures of the House as they related to radio broadcasting and television, after the discussion of the general procedures of the House then underway was concluded. The committee had an opportunity of discussing in a general way last spring the question of broadcasting of House procedures by electronic media and, as a result of these discussions, I understand that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has prepared certain information which will be of assistance to the committee this year, assuming that this motion passes.
May I make some brief references to the actual terms of the motion. It says, among other things, that the standing committee be directed to study the question of radio and television broadcasting in the House, including the legal, procedural and technical aspects thereof. It is obvious that there will be technical problems from the point of view of broadcasting from the chamber itself. This is patently not a forum which lends itself readily to the broadcasting medium, and this motion will give an opportunity for the com-
February 2, 1970
COMMONS DEBATES	3115
mittee to try and solve some of the technical problems.
In addition, the committee must refer to the practice that has grown up in the House of providing facilities for those who report to the radio and television media and interview members outside the Chamber itself. The committee is therefore being asked to examine the arrangements which might be made for the media so that from a technical standpoint radio will be able to obtain a good signal and television a good picture for the purposes of public broadcasting.
A reference is made to the legal considerations involved. I made a number of references to these considerations in the debate last year. Hitherto, the laws of libel and slander have not applied to proceedings inside the House. The proceedings, in such circumstances, have been guided by the principle of parliamentary privilege and, perhaps more important, by the general traditions of the House and have tended to guard against remarks which might be in the nature of slander. Some changes may have to be introduced in this area so that the reputation of no person may be damaged as a result of remarks inside the House or its Committees, that is, so that as a result of anything said by an hon. member inside, no one may be attacked with impunity before the public media and the country. Therefore, the committee will have to look into the legal aspect and the effect on the country's laws of providing for the proceedings of the House and its committees to be broadcast.
Finally, from the procedural standpoint the committee will have to determine what changes in the procedure of the House will be desirable so that the House may have its proceedings broadcast most effectively and so that hon. members, whether in the front benches or the back benches, will have almost equal opportunities to appear. There is an inevitable bias in our system in favour of those sitting in the front benches on either side of the House. The committee will therefore have to consider how to give hon. members on either side comparable opportunities to be heard on a public broadcast.
As I say, the committee will have to consider the proceedings of the House as they now exist in order to see what changes may have to be instituted if we are to adapt to the new medium, just as I assume the proceedings at Westminster had to be adapted some two centuries ago when Mr. Hansard was first
Broadcasting of House of Commons Debates permitted to go into the Commons gallery and take a note of the parliamentary proceedings.
I will delay the House no more, Mr. Speaker. This will be an important step in the history of the Canadian Parlliament. Other parliaments such as that in Westminster have studied this difficult question and pronounced negatively against televising the proceedings of the House. We, in our turn, will have to reach our own decision. I am sure that the committee will bear in mind the observations of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) when he remarked in the debate last March that in this area there is a substantial difference of opinion not so much among parties but among members within parties. On this question I am sure that all hon. members, whether they are members of the committee or not, will have the opportunity to contribute to and involve themselves in the proceedings so that the committee might have the opportunity of hearing their views and arriving at a consensus as to the best method of dealing with this question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: BROADCASTING OF DEBATES BY RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in responding to this motion moved by the minister I think I can say that I was the one who moved the resolution some ten months ago which was referred to by the minister and which formed the basis of a very useful discussion and debate at that time. In concluding his remarks the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) referred to the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who said that not only are there differences among parties but within parties as well. I think this is parallel to the situation that existed in the United Kingdom, where the cleavage was horizontal and ran across party lines. We in this party have a variety of opinions. I think it is proper that this is so. I think it would be very difficult to be otherwise on an issue of this kind, which belongs to the members of the House of Commons. It does not belong to the government. It does not belong to political parties. It is an issue on which for members should be guided by their own conscience, point of view and responsibility and come to a decision. What I have to say will represent my point of view. Other members of my party will have views to offer either in this House or before the committee. I have no doubt that they will vary from the point of view I expressed in the debate ten months ago and which I will again express tonight.
February 2, 1970
3116	COMMONS
Broadcasting of House of Commons Debates
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
It is my hope that when the committee is convened and organized it will, for the purpose of this issue, hold public hearings. During the course of the proceedings when we were considering the proposed rules to be brought before the House, the meetings were held in camera. Whether this was wise or not is beside the point; it is now water under the bridge. I strongly recommend that when the committee is convened and organized its meetings be held in public.
I do not envisage any great rush on the part of the public to attend the meetings, but members of the media who are involved, and interested members of this House, may wish to attend. By that time members of the other place may have completed their own close and interesting examination of the media and may wish to attend the meetings to hear what the House of Commons has to say on the question. I hope this will be the case.
I hope after reasonable consideration, when the committee presents its representations to the House the Whips will not be called upon and individual members will be permitted to vote according to their own point of view. I want to make that quite plain. I know there will be problems. There will be a lot of pain and sutfering attached to either a permanent or experimental introduction of radio and television into this House and its committees. However, I think the benefits will outweight any drawbacks. Nothing is born without pain and suffering. It may well be that members of this House will have to undergo a certain amount of pain and suffering in this regard.
I feel there are two points which must be considered on this issue. What is paramount is the right of the public of Canada who have elected us and in respect of whom we are trustees. The people of Canada have a right to the fullest, most complete and best information which can be obtained from the proceedings of the Parliament of Canada. Many arguments will be made. Some will be very persuasive and some will be convincing as to why it is not a good thing. I will listen with care to those arguments because I am open to persuasion. I think some of the arguments will be the same as those made the time Hansard was introduced into this House several years ago. I think that 20 years after we attempt this timid experiment people will wonder why there was ever any objection to it.
We are not without precedents to observe. Before going on to that however, may I point


out some of the problems which will arise. There is, of course, the problem in his House of the two official languages. This will certainly form a technical problem of considerable size. There is the question of cost. We do not know what that will be. We have some idea of the cost of the experiment which took place in the United Kingdom with relation to the House of Lords. There is the question of the relationship between this House and its committees.
If there is to be an experiment and later a permanent proposal to televise the House and committees, obviously there will have to be some rationalization of the proceedings of both the House and its committees. There is, of course, the very difficult legal problem to which the minister referred which in my opinion will involve remedial changes in the statute. Perhaps I may deal with that question for a moment or two.
I have read the report of the Clerk of the House of the United Kingdom. I have also read the statements and some of the documents in connection with the experiment in Australia with relation to radio, and those in connection with New Zealand. In examining the Senate and House of Commons Act in Canada, sections 4 and 7 explain the privileges and immunities of the members to the actual use by the written media of extracts from official documents of the House. The privileges are extended to cover those, but it is a specific restriction to the written extracts. I think we will probably have to follow the same practice with regard to privilege as exists in the United Kingdom.
I will give an example. Perhaps even on an experimental basis the proceedings of this House or its committees may be televised or broadcast by radio. A statement made in this House is of course protected by the traditional rights and privileges of members of the House. If the proceedings are being broadcast live, and a statement is made which could well have a slanderous effect, although it is protected in this House, what would be the position of the member or the network which broadcast the slanderous statement which was received outside the House?
In spite of what was said in New Zealand, this seems to be a legal proposition. It might well be that we will have some trouble. Apart from the question of fair comment, there is some likelihood of being sued for slander. If we are going to do this, I hope the committee
February 2, 1970	COMMONS
will receive adequate legal advice and will review the proposals made in Australia and the United Kingdom. I hope the committee will consider the excellent and learned article by the Clerk of the United Kingdom House. I hope it will take a hard look at the necessity of amending the Senate and House of Commons Act.
I will now deal with the question of merits.
I know the problems, technical and otherwise, which will result. I know it will probably be a long, hard, arduous and difficult process to evolve a system which will be acceptable to all members. I think it would be best if the committee recommended a trial period of radio broadcasting. Australia has almost 25 years' experience in radio broadcasting, and some limited experience in televising. Despite the fact that the arguments advanced in Australia in 1945 and 1946 paralleled the arguments advanced by people in the United Kingdom at the time of the proposal to inaugurate a written record of the proceedings of the House, the Australian people have now come to accept this system-radio broadcasting in particular.
I am not suggesting there is any great national outcry that proceedings of this House of Commons, the other place or the committees of either are essential for entertainment, amusement and the advancement of the knowledge of the people of Canada. What has been happening in the past is that by a gradual process which at times we were not able to perceive, the emphasis on Parliament has been slowly moving out of this chamber and into other places. I am not about to rehash the problems that Your Honour and others have had in connection with the difficulties of the electronic media. Radio and television reporters have attempted to obtain clarification and expansion from members of this House of statements made here and repeated outside.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The trouble is that this practice developed in the course of a year or so to a point at which in the minds of a great many Canadians there was some doubt whether what took place in this chamber, or immediately afterwards outside it, constituted in fact the proceedings of the House of Commons. It is probable that no one was at fault. The practice just grew; it just came about. The Chair finally came to a wise decision. All the decisions which the Chair makes are wise, of course, particularly since there is now no
DEBATES	3117
Broadcasting of House of Commons Debates right of appeal against Your Honour's rulings..
I did not mean that to be a backhanded compliment. The fact is we were in grave danger of losing the usefulness and advantages of this democratic institution of the House of: Commons.
There will still, of course, have to be means by which members of this House can be requested, under suitable arrangements satisfactory to all concerned, to explain and amplify statements made here. I hope we will not then be met with the situation which arose when we attempted to raise in this House questions of privilege, or challenge statements made outside. When we tried to do this we were advised, and quite properly according to the precedents, that we were not able to proceed along those lines. I should like to think that having examined some of the statements made in the House and some of the statements of clarification made outside, the committee would find itself able to examine this question of privilege in relation to the connection between the two.
The other point I should like to make is this. Because of the diversity and size of our country we do not possess what is known as a national press. It is no one's fault. There is, of course, the Canadian Press, and there are a number of writers and commentators covering events on a national basis. But we tend to take a regional approach to events. Much of the press gives greatest prominence to matter which are of the greatest interest to particular cities or regions. This is natural, and it is obviously the case. I suggest this is why an increasing interest has developed in national television and radio coverage; it is because these media have instant access to a national audience, and because what was said or televised outside this chamber had more national significance than the articles which appeared in the press.
This is another reason for considering the advantages of continuing the practice in some form, since they may well outweigh the disadvantages. Indeed, in my view the advantages of tackling this problem along experimental lines do, indeed, outweigh the disadvantages. I hope sufficient hon. members will agree wlith me in this regard.
I said earlier that I would mention the situation in Australia and in New Zealand. I was particularly interested in a statement by the late Sir Gilbert Campion, the well-known.

February 2, 1970
Business of the House
Clerk of the United Kingdom House, who had this to say on a visit to New Zealand in 1949: If one considers only the popular reaction, the experiment of broadcasting debates would seem to have justified itself. People have learned much more about the purposes and proceedings of Parliament. Some are shocked to find that the tone of a democratic assembly is not that of an areopagus or a Roman senate. Many have developed a live interest in the debates and both parties agree that discontinuance is unthinkable.
Another interesting comment was made by an Australian visiting New Zealand who happened to turn the radio onto the wavelength which covered the proceedings broadcast from the New Zealand legislature. His comment was the kind one would expect to hear. He said that the speeches might not have been of the highest quality, and there were probably mistakes in the syntax and in the English, but they had an agreeable element of spontaneity. The interruptions, the arguments and the questions were a spontaneous reflection of the people in the chamber who, in their turn, represented the people of the country as this man summed it up, "This house is the people of New Zealand with all their virtues, all their defects, all their warts."
I realize there will be a long and arduous period of experimentation before us, but in my view we cannot struggle against the fact that this is a medium which no one can escape, and one which offers advantages. Nevertheless, I think we should be most careful that whatever results will have its origin in a logical basis acceptable for a trial period to all of us. I hope the committee will undertake its task with this thought in mind and make its report in an objective wtay to face a good, freewheeling debate with, hopefully, a free vote at its conclusion.

HOUSING-1970 CONSTRUCTION TARGET FOR HOMES FOR ELDERLY AND THOSE ON LOW INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, right after the Christmas recess I reminded the minister in charge of housing that last year the federal government gave direct assistance under the National Housing Act to the building of some 20,000 dwellings for elderly and low-income people with families. I asked him what the target was for 1970. We were glad to have the suspense ended this afternoon when he answered that funds would be available to construct
35,000	housing units specifically for low-income families. Although this total is greater than last year's, it still falls far short of the need. In Toronto alone I am told there is a waiting list of 15,000 applicants, enough to take up almost half the number of units to be provided for all Canada.
Since the minister answered my question this afternoon, I want to do something rather unusual and ask him further questions so as to get a march on his next statement in the House. The hon. gentleman's statement raised fully as many questions as it answered. I am glad he promised to make a detailed statement soon, and I should like to draw his attention to some of the questions which people are still waiting to hear answered.
[DOT] (10.00 p.m.)
The first relates to my question this afternoon. Can the minister assure us that all these 35,000 new, low-income dwellings will have modern facilities for the recreational needs of the tenants of all ages, both inside and outside the housing units? If people with good incomes need space for play and other leisure activities, people with low incomes need this a great deal more. People with good incomes can get away and find the recreation, the space and places for other activities they require. People with low incomes are forced
February 2, 1970	COMMONS
to stay, and consequently their needs are very much greater. They have fewer advantages and their needs and the needs of the whole community by extension are greater.
My second question: When does the minister propose to announce the new rental scale for public housing which has been hanging fire for so long? To be an improvement over the existing one it needs to be based on net income, not gross income as at present. A single-parent mother, to mention only one type, needs to be able to deduct the cost of child care before the rent is calculated, and to be able to deduct other legitimate expenses. Otherwise there is no use whatsoever in expecting that such families can get off welfare and back into the living and working stream of the community.
A Canadian Welfare Council survey last year found that mothers on welfare across Canada, single-parent mothers with four children, to give one example, spent half their income on rent. That is out of all reason. A rent of that dimension leaves too little for the other needs of the family.
My third question: Is the minister giving consideration to a program of outright grants to enable low income homeowners to improve their older homes? These people simply cannot repay loans and the interest on them. There is no use in the minister saying we already have legislation to cover these people. The grants could be made returnable on the death of the owner and/or the sale of the house, but they must be grants and not loans.
My fourth question:	The minister
announced that the allocation for student housing is to be $45 million this year compared with $55 million last year. Does he really consider this 20 per cent drop a "modest decline" as he says? Faced with the need to repay student loans, and with the bleak prospect for summer jobs ahead, a good many students will be hard put to it to get the education they need and which Canada needs them to have.
All these people on low income, and many other types, need proper housing now. They need it so that they can support their families in modern homes with the attractions that keep families together. They need it so they can afford to go out and get the training and the jobs that will make them part of the community and will give them self-respect and the right to carry their share of the load. They need it to keep their homes in repair in order to live out their lives in comfort.

It is all very well to talk about the war on inflation, but a war on inflation ought not to be carried to such lengths as to become a war on the poor by refusing to extend housing to the required amount. POST OFFICE-FINANCIAL POSITION FOLLOWING INCREASED RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry but I thought three questions would be discussed this evening.
Here is the question I put to the Postmaster General: Have his decisions with regard to new postal rates and new working conditions for postal employees finally put the Canadian postal service on a profit-earning basis?
It will be recalled how protests greeted the increase from 5 to 6 cents in the postal rate for first class mail. It will also be recalled how all newspapers and magazines, especially weeklies and monthly publications, protested vehemently for being thus threatened with bankruptcy.
In fact, protests are still being raised. A number of magazines and weeklies which were already in a difficult position though acknowledgely excellent have disappeared or are bound to do so very soon.

Several trades and industries rely, for their publicity, on the efficiency of the postal service. What has happened since the day these decisions were made?
People are complaining. The delivery of second and third class mail is slow. In the urban districts, the fact that services are discontinued from Friday night on is bringing a lot of other services to a standstill.
Last year, I sent to my electors in La Tuque a notice calling them to a meeting. Imagine my surprise on discovering that I had arrived in La Tuque before my notice!
Where are all these changes leading to. Mr. Speaker? Has the volume of mail increased? And the number of money orders, of registered letters and other postal matter?
[DOT] (10.10 p.m.)
Should good service everywhere not be the foremost objective? Should some areas be deprived of postal service for a matter of earnings?
I am under the impression that the minister went the wrong way about it, but stubborn as any good Irishman, he may not be willing to admit it.
The minister should inform the House as soon as possible whether his department is moving ahead or losing ground. I know one can always juggle with figures. I do not want to be given just any figures. I wish to be provided with statistics I can compare with those of the 1967-68 financial year.
I am convinced that the Canadian postal service is losing a lot of money and I should like the minister to contradict me. I would be happy if he could.
All newspapers and magazines, all businesses and industries are striving hard to discover new means of distribution other than those of the post office.
I think that the postal service will become less and less economical, and, once more, further rate increases will be suggested.
Therefore, I ask the minister to tell us whether the decisions taken last year have been effective.
